# A Reader's Introduction {.unnumbered}

Jude is easy to miss. It sits just before Revelation, a single chapter of twenty-five verses, and in the Greek text that underlies this book it runs to about 460 words. Most people could read it aloud in under three minutes. Many Christians know only its closing benediction, "Now to him that is able to keep you from falling" (v. 24, WBS), and perhaps its call to "contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints" (v. 3, WEB). The middle of the letter (fallen angels, an archangel quarrelling with the Devil over a corpse, a prophecy from Enoch, reefs, clouds, uprooted trees, and stars that have wandered from their paths) can seem so strange that readers hurry past it.

This book is written for readers who would rather slow down.

Jude rewards slowness because it is so compressed. Almost every phrase calls up a story, a scripture, or a tradition that its first readers knew well and we mostly do not. "The way of Cain" assumes a whole history of how Jewish interpreters understood Cain. "Clouds without water" assumes a farmer's dread of a rainless sky. "Love feasts" assumes a practice of shared meals in early Christian communities that most churches no longer keep in that form. When Jude names Michael and Moses' body, or quotes "Enoch, the seventh from Adam," he speaks the language of a world of Jewish scriptural interpretation that has its own texts, conventions, and arguments. Unfold those references and the letter changes from a cryptic rant into a carefully built piece of pastoral persuasion. It is written with real literary skill, steeped in Israel's scriptures, and aimed at keeping a community together in the love of God.

## What this book is

*Jude, Unfolded* is an expository commentary: a guided walk through the text, verse by verse and phrase by phrase. It sets out to explain:

- **what the text says**, in the Greek in which Jude wrote it, as the earliest manuscripts preserve it, and in many English translations;
- **what it likely meant** to its first readers, given their scriptures, customs, and situation;
- **why it may have been said that way**, which means attending to Jude's images, his rhetorical patterns, and his choices among traditions;
- **how it may be responsibly applied today**, kept clearly separate from the explanation of what the text meant.

Along the way the book stops for **deep dives**, longer explorations of subjects that modern readers rarely meet elsewhere. A reader who wonders "What exactly was a love feast?" will find a full answer in Chapter 6, drawn from the New Testament and from the earliest Christian and Roman writers who describe such meals. The same care goes to the Book of Enoch, the dispute over Moses' body, the wandering stars, the "faith once delivered," and more than a dozen other subjects.

## How the chapters work

After the introductory chapters, each of the thirteen main chapters follows the same pattern, so you can always find your way:

- **A. The Text**: the passage in Greek, a table of what the earliest manuscripts read, and every verse in eighteen free English translations.
- **B. Plain-English Orientation**: the big picture before the details.
- **C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration**: the heart of each chapter. Each heading gives a Greek phrase, its transliteration, and a plain rendering in single quotation marks.
- **D. Original-Language Investigation**: the Greek words that matter, explained for readers who know no Greek.
- **E. The Historical and Cultural World**: the customs, beliefs, and institutions the text assumes.
- **F. Connections Across Scripture**: quotations, allusions, and shared themes, each explained.
- **G. Scholarly and Theological Questions**: where interpreters disagree, and why.
- **H. The Passage Within Jude**: how this section advances the letter's argument.
- **I. Contemporary Understanding**: possible implications for faith and life today.
- **J. Reflection and Discussion**: questions for personal study or groups.
- **K. Sources**: the notes behind the chapter's claims.
- **L. Texts Highlighted in This Chapter**: every passage of Scripture (and of 1 Enoch and the Apocrypha) that the chapter cites or alludes to, printed in full in the original language and in two English translations. References in the chapter link to these entries.

You do not need to read every section in order. A small group might read A, B, C, and I together, use J for discussion, and leave D and G to members who want more detail. A preacher or teacher will probably want everything. Section L is there to be consulted: when a chapter says that Jude echoes the rebellion of Korah or the vision of Joshua the high priest, the passage itself is a click or a few pages away.

## The original first, and many translations

Jude wrote in Greek, and his letter reached us through handwritten copies. This book therefore starts every passage with the Greek text, and it gives priority to the manuscripts themselves. Section A of each chapter shows what ten of the earliest and most important manuscripts actually read, from papyri copied in the third or fourth century to the ninth- and tenth-century copies that stand behind most later texts. The readings are checked against published transcriptions of the manuscripts, not taken on trust. When the commentary turns to the Old Testament, it reads the Hebrew (and, where Jude seems to have known it, the Greek Septuagint).

No English translation is treated as more important than another. Each verse of Jude is printed in eighteen free translations, from William Tyndale's New Testament of 1534 to translations completed in the last few years, in order of first publication. Some are strictly word-for-word (Young's Literal Translation, the Literal Standard Version, the Unlocked Literal Bible); some aim at natural modern English (the Berean Standard Bible, the Open English Bible, the Free Bible Version); one, the Translation for Translators, spells out meaning the Greek leaves implicit. Reading them side by side shows where translators agree, where they must choose, and why. When the commentary quotes another passage of Scripture, it names the translation it quotes, and it often uses a literal one so that the structure of the original stays visible. Section L then prints that passage in full in its original language and in the Berean Standard Bible and the World English Bible, two public-domain translations that between them follow both of the main forms of the Greek text.

Every text in this book is in the public domain or under a free license. That is a principle, not an accident: Scripture should be free to read, copy, translate, and share, and so should a book that tries to open it. Translations whose publishers require permission, such as the ESV, NASB, NLT, the Amplified Bible, and *The Message*, are therefore not quoted. The Copyright and Licensing page explains this and lists the free translations that cover the same range.

## What you will not need

You will not need to know Greek. Every Greek word appears with a transliteration and a plain explanation. You will not need a theological education; technical terms are explained when they first appear and collected in the Glossary. You will not need to agree with every conclusion. Where good interpreters disagree, this book tries to set out the options fairly and to show the evidence on each side, so you can weigh them for yourself.

## A word about the tone of Jude

Jude can sound harsh. It speaks of judgment, fire, and darkness, and it describes certain people in vivid and unflattering images. Some readers find this off-putting, and others find it attractive for the wrong reasons. This book takes the severity of Jude seriously without making it the whole story. The letter begins with readers who are "called, … loved, … and … kept," and it ends with praise to the God who is able to keep them from stumbling. Its last practical words are about mercy, rescue, and compassion for those who are wavering. The darkness of the middle section stands inside a frame of love, and the letter cannot be read rightly without both.

Jude wanted, by his own account, to write about "our common salvation" (v. 3). Circumstances forced him to write a warning instead. Even so, the salvation he wanted to celebrate shines through the warning, and helping you see it is the purpose of this book.


# Research Method and Interpretive Principles {.unnumbered}

A commentary is only as trustworthy as the way it was made. This chapter sets out how this book was researched, what kinds of sources stand behind its claims, and the principles that guided interpretation. Readers who want to get straight to the text can skip ahead and come back later. Readers who want to know how far to trust what follows should read on.

## Sources and how they were used

Every source behind this book is free: in the public domain or under a Creative Commons license that allows anyone to copy and adapt it. That rule was applied strictly. Where a useful modern work could not be quoted freely, or could not be checked directly during the research, it was left out, and the point it would have supported was either established from a free source or not made.

The sources are used in a fixed order of priority.

**1. The manuscripts.** Jude's words reach us through handwritten copies, so the manuscripts come first. For ten of the earliest and most important witnesses (the papyri P72 and P78, the great fourth- and fifth-century codices ℵ, A, B, and C, and the later manuscripts K, L, Ψ, and 1739), the book reads the transcriptions published by the Institute for New Testament Textual Research in Münster. Every reading reported in a manuscript table was checked by a script against those transcriptions.

**2. The Greek and Hebrew texts.** The Greek text printed and discussed is the SBL Greek New Testament, edited by Michael W. Holmes, with its apparatus of variant readings. An updated form of that apparatus records where the Nestle–Aland 28th edition (NA28) differs. The Byzantine text (Robinson–Pierpont, 2018) and the Textus Receptus are compared throughout. Old Testament passages are read in the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex and, where Jude seems to depend on it, in the Greek of the Septuagint.

**3. Translations, with no favorite.** Eighteen free English translations, from 1534 to 2022, are printed for every verse of Jude. They are quoted exactly from their electronic editions, and a script checks every quotation in the book against the translation it names. The commentary often quotes a literal translation when it is explaining the structure of a Greek or Hebrew sentence. That is a choice made for clarity in a particular place, not a judgment that one translation is better than the others.

**4. Ancient sources.** When Jude alludes to a Jewish or early Christian tradition, the book goes back to the ancient text itself in a free edition: 1 Enoch in R. H. Charles's translation, the Targums in J. W. Etheridge's, Josephus in William Whiston's, the Septuagint and the Apocrypha in Brenton's edition, and the church fathers in the nineteenth-century *Ante-Nicene* and *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* translations. Each passage relied on was read directly. The notes give book, chapter, and section so that readers can check them.

**5. Lexical data.** Greek word meanings are drawn mainly from G. Abbott-Smith's *Manual Greek Lexicon of the New Testament* (1922). It is a public-domain lexicon that summarizes the classical, Septuagint, and papyrus evidence for each New Testament word. Word counts and grammatical data were computed directly from the MorphGNT edition of the SBLGNT, so a statement such as "this word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament" rests on a count of the actual text.

**6. Older commentaries.** Commentators of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries did careful work on Jude, and their books are now in the public domain. This book cites J. B. Mayor (*Expositor's Greek Testament*, 1910), Alfred Plummer (in *Ellicott's Commentary* and the *Expositor's Bible*), E. H. Plumptre (*Cambridge Bible*), J. E. Huther (Meyer series), the *Pulpit Commentary*, and others, always quoting them directly from the text consulted. Where their views have been overtaken by later evidence, such as the discovery among the Dead Sea Scrolls of Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch, the book says so. For facts that are well established but postdate these authors, it cites the relevant Wikipedia article (CC BY-SA), identified by title.

The full **source ledger**, which records what was verified, how, and what remains uncertain, is part of the project files that accompany the manuscript, together with the scripts that generate and check the texts.

## Principles of interpretation

**1. The text has the first word.** Fidelity to Scripture comes before defending any preferred interpretation. Where a popular reading does not fit Jude's words, the book says so, even when that reading is cherished.

**2. Meaning before application.** Each chapter separates what the text meant in its first setting from how it may be applied now. The two are related, but they are not the same thing, and confusing them is the source of much misuse of Jude.

**3. Kinds of claims are labeled.** The book tries to make clear whether a statement is a textual fact ("the Greek word occurs only here"), historical evidence ("Pliny reports…"), scholarly consensus, a contested interpretation, a theological tradition, a plausible inference, or a suggested application. Historical reconstructions, however likely, are presented as reconstructions.

**4. Words mean what they mean in use.** A Greek word's meaning is determined by how it was actually used in its period, not by its etymology or by adding up its parts. The book points out etymologies when they are interesting and warns when they have been overworked. For example, ἐκκλησία does not mean "the called-out ones" just because it contains the parts "out" and "call." Jude's word σπιλάδες, discussed in Chapter 6, is a good example of a word whose sense must be settled by usage.

**5. Traditions outside the Bible are taken seriously and handled carefully.** Jude quotes 1 Enoch and alludes to a tradition about Michael and Moses that appears nowhere in the Old Testament. The book does not explain these away. It shows where they come from, how Jude uses them, and how the church has argued about what that use implies. Quoting a text is not the same as endorsing everything in it, and the book is careful not to claim more than Jude does.

**6. Disagreements are presented fairly.** When responsible scholars disagree, the book sets out the main options, the evidence for each, and their strengths and weaknesses. It sometimes states a preference and gives reasons, but it tries to give readers what they need to decide differently.

**7. No denominational polemics.** Christians read Jude within many traditions. Where those traditions differ in ways that affect the meaning, for example on the "brothers" of Jesus or on how believers are "kept," the book describes the differences without taking sides in old quarrels.

**8. The letter stays whole.** Word studies serve the reading of the letter and do not replace it. Each chapter ends by placing its passage in the flow of Jude's argument, and the overview chapter maps the whole.

## About the Greek

Greek words appear in Greek script with a transliteration in italics, for example ἀγάπη (*agapē*). The transliteration follows a simple scholarly system: η = *ē*, ω = *ō*, υ = *y* (*u* in diphthongs), χ = *ch*, θ = *th*, φ = *ph*, ψ = *ps*, and rough breathing = *h*. Readers who do not read Greek can ignore the Greek script and follow the transliteration and explanation. Grammatical terms are explained when they first appear and collected in the Glossary.

A few grammatical ideas recur often enough to introduce here:

- **Tense and aspect.** Greek verb forms say less about *when* an action happens than English tenses do and more about *how* the action is viewed. The **perfect** presents a completed action with continuing results ("having been loved," and still loved). The **aorist** presents an action as a whole, without comment on its duration. The **present** presents an action as ongoing or in progress.
- **Participles** are verbal adjectives ("having been called," "praying"). Jude uses them heavily, and much of his meaning rides on them.
- **The optative** is a verb form used to express wishes ("may mercy … be multiplied"). It is rare in the New Testament, and Jude uses it twice.
- **Cases** (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative) mark a noun's role in the sentence. The **dative** in particular can mean "to," "for," "by," or "in," and Jude's first verse depends on which is chosen.

## About the variant readings

The New Testament survives in thousands of handwritten manuscripts, and they differ in small and sometimes significant ways. Jude has more than its share of interesting variants. One of them changes who is said to have led Israel out of Egypt, and another changes the shape of the letter's final instructions. The book explains the significant variants where they arise and gathers them in Appendix A. Readers should know that none of these variants touches the substance of the Christian faith. Some do, however, affect how particular verses are read, and they deserve honest explanation.

## About application

The "Contemporary Understanding" sections suggest ways Jude's message may inform belief, worship, fellowship, ethics, and spiritual practice today. They are offered as possibilities to weigh, not as divine instructions. Jude was written against particular people doing particular things, and it is easy to aim its sharpest words at whoever we happen to dislike. The book tries to resist that temptation and to let Jude question its readers, this author included, before it is turned on anyone else.


# Historical and Literary Introduction to Jude {.unnumbered}

Before walking through Jude verse by verse, it helps to ask the questions any careful reader asks of an ancient letter. Who wrote it? When, and to whom? What was happening that made it necessary? What kind of writing is it, and what world of ideas does it assume? How did the early church receive it? For a letter as short as Jude, the answers are often less certain than we would like. The evidence is still worth laying out, both for what it shows and for what it leaves open.

## 1. "Judas … brother of James": who wrote the letter?

The letter opens:

> Judas, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, …
>
> — Jude 1, LSV

The Greek name Ἰούδας (*Ioudas*) is the Greek form of the Hebrew *Yehudah*, Judah, the name of Jacob's fourth son and of the tribe and land descended from him. English Bibles usually write "Jude" for the author of this letter. The convention distinguishes him from Judas Iscariot, but the Greek name is the same, and the LSV keeps "Judas." The name was very common among Jews of the period, so the author's identity depends on the clue he gives: he is the "brother of James."

### The candidates

Several men named Judas appear in the New Testament:

1. **Judas the brother of Jesus.** Mark lists him among Jesus' brothers: "Is this not the carpenter, the Son of Mary, and brother of James, and Joses, and Judas, and Simon?" ([Mark 6:3](#hl-hist-mrk-6), LSV; cf. [Matt 13:55](#hl-hist-mat-13)).
2. **Judas "of James,"** one of the Twelve, listed by Luke: "Judas of James, and Judas Iscariot, who also became betrayer" ([Luke 6:16](#hl-hist-luk-6), LSV; cf. [Acts 1:13](#hl-hist-act-1)). John calls him "Judas … (not the Iscariot)" ([John 14:22](#hl-hist-jhn-14), LSV). The Greek Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου most naturally means "Judas son of James," which is the usual way of using a genitive with a personal name. It does not mean "brother of James."
3. **Judas called Barsabbas**, a prophet and leader in the Jerusalem church who carried the apostolic letter to Antioch ([Acts 15:22, 32](#hl-hist-act-15)).
4. **Judas Thomas**, a figure of later Syriac Christian tradition in which the apostle Thomas ("twin") is named Judas.

Among these, the first is the only one for whom "brother of James" is a natural self-description. Only one James in early Christianity was famous enough to identify someone simply by naming him: James of Jerusalem, "the brother of the LORD" ([Gal 1:19](#hl-hist-gal-1), LSV). Paul names him as one of the "pillars" of the Jerusalem church ([Gal 2:9](#hl-hist-gal-2)). He leads the council in [Acts 15](#hl-hist-act-15) and receives Paul in [Acts 21:18](#hl-hist-act-21), and tradition takes him to be the author of the Letter of James, who also calls himself simply "a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" ([Jas 1:1](#hl-hist-jas-1), LSV). A Judas who introduces himself as "brother of James" is almost certainly claiming to be the brother of *that* James, and so a brother of Jesus.

### Why "brother of James" and not "brother of the Lord"?

If Jude was the brother of Jesus, why did he not say so? Ancient readers asked the same question. Clement of Alexandria, writing around AD 200, answered with a comment that later readers have found persuasive:

> Jude, who wrote the Catholic Epistle, the brother of the sons of Joseph, and very religious, while knowing the near relationship of the Lord, yet did not say that he himself was His brother. But what said he? Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ,—of Him as Lord; but the brother of James.[^i-1]

Several factors probably worked together. The family relationship was no longer the defining fact; after the resurrection, Jesus' brothers came to know him as Lord. The Gospels remember that during Jesus' ministry "not even His brothers were believing in Him" ([John 7:5](#hl-hist-jhn-7), LSV). Yet after Easter they appear among the praying disciples ([Acts 1:14](#hl-hist-act-1)), and Paul knows that the risen Christ "appeared to James" ([1 Cor 15:7](#hl-hist-1co-15), LSV). A brother by birth who had become a servant by faith might well prefer to call himself the second. Naming James also placed Jude within a recognized line of authority without claiming the title of apostle, which he appears to reserve for others (v. 17).

### The family of Jesus in early tradition

Two pieces of evidence outside the Gospels fill out the picture.

First, Paul mentions in passing that "the brothers of the LORD" traveled on missionary work with their wives ([1 Cor 9:5](#hl-hist-1co-9), LSV). That remark, written in the mid-50s, shows that at least some of Jesus' brothers besides James were known as traveling preachers among the churches. Jude, who writes to readers he knows and who are at some distance from him, fits that profile.

Second, the second-century Jewish-Christian writer Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, tells a story about Jude's grandsons. When the emperor Domitian (reigned AD 81–96) feared the descendants of David, "the grandchildren of Jude, who is said to have been the Lord's brother according to the flesh," were brought before him. They owned a small farm worth nine thousand denarii, showed him the calluses on their hands from working it, and explained that Christ's kingdom was "not a temporal nor an earthly kingdom, but a heavenly and angelic one." Domitian let them go as harmless. Afterward, Hegesippus says, they "ruled the churches because they were witnesses and were also relatives of the Lord," and they lived until the time of Trajan.[^i-2] The story probably includes some legendary color, but it preserves a memory of Jude's family as Galilean farmers, rooted in Jewish Christianity and respected in the churches.

### Deep dive: who were Jesus' "brothers"?

The New Testament names four brothers of Jesus (James, Joses or Joseph, Judas, and Simon) and mentions sisters ([Mark 6:3](#hl-hist-mrk-6)). Christians have understood these relationships in three main ways, and the differences matter for how readers picture Jude.

- **Full brothers (the "Helvidian" view, after Helvidius, a fourth-century writer).** On this view they were children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus. Most Protestant interpreters hold it, pointing to the plain sense of the word ἀδελφός (*adelphos*) and to texts such as [Matt 1:25](#hl-hist-mat-1).
- **Older half-brothers, sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (the "Epiphanian" view, after Epiphanius of Salamis).** This view is attested in second-century writings. It has been common in Eastern Orthodox tradition and fits Clement's description of Jude as "the brother of the sons of Joseph."
- **Cousins (the "Hieronymian" view, after Jerome).** This view takes *adelphos* in the broader sense of "kinsman," a sense it can carry in Jewish usage. It became standard in the Latin West and is common in Roman Catholic interpretation.

All three views agree on what matters most for this book: Jude belonged to Jesus' own family circle, grew up near him, and came to call him "Master and Lord" (v. 4). Readers who hold different views of Mary can read Jude in the same way.

### Did Jude himself write it?

Many scholars accept that the letter was written by Jude, the brother of Jesus. Many others think it was written later by someone using his name, a practice called pseudonymity that was known in the ancient world. The main arguments for a later writer are these:

- **The Greek is good.** Jude's vocabulary is rich, with sixteen words found nowhere else in the New Testament, and his style is vivid and carefully patterned. Could a Galilean villager write like this?
- **"The faith once delivered" (v. 3)** is said to treat Christianity as a fixed body of doctrine, which some regard as typical of a later, more institutional stage.
- **The apostles seem to belong to the past** (v. 17).

Defenders of authenticity reply:

- **Greek was widely used in Galilee**, and a family whose members traveled as missionaries in the Greek-speaking world ([1 Cor 9:5](#hl-hist-1co-9)) had every opportunity to learn it well. Ancient authors also commonly used secretaries, who could polish style. The quality of the Greek is a real question, but it does not settle authorship.
- **"The faith" as the content of the Christian message** already appears in Paul's earliest letters: "he who is persecuting us then, now proclaims good news—the faith that he was then destroying" ([Gal 1:23](#hl-hist-gal-1), LSV). Language about "delivering" teaching is also early ([1 Cor 11:2; 15:3](#hl-hist-1co-11)).
- **Verse 17 asks readers to remember what the apostles told *them***. That requires only that the apostles had preached to these readers earlier, not that they were all long dead.
- **The choice of name is the strongest argument.** A later writer who wanted authority would hardly choose an obscure figure like Jude, and having chosen him, would likely have added the impressive title "brother of the Lord." A modest self-description fits the real Jude better than an imitator.

This book treats authorship by Jude the brother of Jesus as a responsible conclusion that fits the evidence well. It does not regard the question as closed, and very little of the letter's interpretation depends on the answer.[^i-3]

## 2. Language and style

Jude writes a compact, energetic, and artful Greek. Several features stand out, and they will recur throughout this book:

- **Rare words.** Of about 226 distinct words in Jude, sixteen occur nowhere else in the New Testament, among them the words meaning ‘contend for’ (v. 3), ‘slip in’ (v. 4), ‘reefs’ (v. 12), ‘late-autumn’ (v. 12), ‘foam up’ (v. 13), ‘wanderers’ (v. 13), ‘grumblers’ and ‘fault-finders’ (v. 16), ‘make divisions’ (v. 19), and ‘without stumbling’ (v. 24).[^i-4]
- **Triads.** Jude thinks in threes: called, loved, kept (v. 1); mercy, peace, love (v. 2); three examples of judgment (vv. 5–7); three sins of the ‘dreamers’ (v. 8); Cain, Balaam, Korah (v. 11); three groups to whom mercy is shown (vv. 22–23).
- **Catchwords.** Key words return in new settings and bind the letter together. The clearest is "keep" (τηρέω, *tēreō*): the readers are "kept" (v. 1), the angels did not "keep" their position and are "kept" for judgment (v. 6), darkness is "kept" for the wandering stars (v. 13), and the readers are to "keep" themselves in God's love (v. 21) as they trust the God who is able to "guard" them (v. 24).
- **The "these" pattern.** After each example or prophecy, Jude turns to the troublemakers with "these" (οὗτοι, *houtoi*): "those dreaming" (v. 8, where the LSV renders the word "those"), "these, indeed, whatever [things] they have not known" (v. 10), "These are stains" (v. 12), "These are … grumblers" (v. 16), "these are those causing divisions" (v. 19).
- **Vivid images drawn from nature and from Israel's story.**

## 3. Date and setting

The letter gives no explicit date. If Jude the brother of Jesus wrote it, it was written within his lifetime, probably before the 90s and possibly much earlier, since Hegesippus's story about Domitian concerns his grandsons. Some scholars date it to the 50s or early 60s, which would make it one of the earliest New Testament writings. Others place it between 70 and 100. The letter's horizon is strikingly Jewish and apocalyptic. It never mentions the destruction of Jerusalem's temple (AD 70), but arguments from silence are weak in so short a letter.

This uncertainty affects the interpretation less than one might expect. Jude's concerns are about holding to the received faith, moral integrity, authority, divisive teachers, and mercy toward the wavering. Those concerns fit the first Christian century at almost any point.

## 4. The recipients

Jude addresses "those called, having been loved … and having been kept" (v. 1), a description of all believers rather than of a particular place. Yet the letter is clearly written to particular people: he calls them "beloved" three times (vv. 3, 17, 20). He knows that intruders have slipped into their community (v. 4) and sit at their love feasts (v. 12), and he can remind them of what the apostles had told them (vv. 17–18).

He also assumes that they will understand compressed references to the exodus, to fallen angels, to Michael and Moses, to Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and to the prophecy of Enoch. Such readers were most likely Jewish Christians, or a mixed community deeply formed by Jewish scriptural interpretation. Suggested locations include Palestine, Syria, Egypt, and Asia Minor. None can be proven, and this book does not build on any of them.

## 5. The troublemakers

Jude does not name the people he opposes. He calls them "certain men" (v. 4), and everything we know about them comes from his description. Gathering his charges gives this profile:

- They are **inside** the community. They "came in … stealthily" (v. 4) and share its meals (v. 12).
- They turn **grace into license**, especially sexual license (vv. 4, 7–8, 16, 18).
- They **deny** Jesus Christ as Master and Lord, probably by the way they live rather than by explicit doctrinal denial (v. 4).
- They appeal to **dreams**, apparently claimed revelations (v. 8).
- They **reject authority** and **slander glorious beings** (vv. 8–10).
- They are **self-serving**, "shepherding themselves" (v. 12), "for the sake of profit" (v. 16), like Balaam "for reward" (v. 11).
- They are **divisive** and, in Jude's judgment, **"not having the Spirit"** (v. 19).

Older commentators often identified them as Gnostics, members of the second-century movements that taught salvation through secret knowledge and despised the material world. The resemblance is partial at best. Jude says nothing about a lower creator-god, a cosmic myth, or a doctrine of secret knowledge. The developed Gnostic systems also belong to a later period than most scholars assign to Jude. The *Pulpit Commentary* already judged that nothing in the letter warrants the supposition that Jude "was thinking of Simon Magus in particular, or of Carpocrates, or any of the early Gnostics," though it allowed that "the seeds which were to develop into the pronounced Gnosticism of a later time were already sown."[^i-5] Jude's own charges suggest something simpler: traveling teachers who claimed prophetic or charismatic authority and taught that grace freed believers from moral law. That picture is this book's reconstruction, built from Jude's words and from early Christian instructions for testing traveling prophets (Chapter 2), and the book treats it as a reconstruction.

## 6. What kind of writing is Jude?

Jude is a **letter**. It has the standard opening (sender, recipients, greeting) and an elaborate closing doxology in place of the usual farewell. In substance it is a **sermon or word of exhortation in letter form**, with a clear rhetorical aim: to move its hearers to "fight for the faith" (v. 3).

Two ways of describing its structure are especially illuminating:

- **A Jewish interpretive pattern.** The central section (vv. 5–19) alternates between *texts* (scriptural examples, a tradition, a prophecy, an apostolic prediction) and *interpretations* introduced by "these" (οὗτοι). J. B. Mayor, following F. H. Chase, noted that the formula οὗτοί εἰσιν ("these are") belongs to apocalyptic writing that explains visions. Zechariah's angel says, "These [are] they whom YHWH has sent" ([Zech 1:10](#hl-hist-zec-1), LSV), and Revelation's elder says, "These are those who are coming out of the Great Tribulation" ([Rev 7:14](#hl-hist-rev-7), LSV). Mayor suggested that Jude adopted the formula from such writings.[^i-6] The pattern also resembles the *pesher* commentaries among the Dead Sea Scrolls, which quote a prophetic text and then explain its "interpretation" in terms of the community's own time.[^i-6b] It suggests a writer trained in Jewish ways of reading Scripture as prophecy fulfilled in his own day.
- **Greco-Roman rhetoric.** Ancient teachers of speech described the parts of a persuasive address. Quintilian, writing in the first century AD, reports that "most authorities divide the forensic speech into five parts: the exordium, the statement of facts, the proof, the refutation, and the peroration."[^i-7] Read with these categories, Jude has an introduction stating its purpose (v. 3), a statement of the situation (v. 4), the proofs (vv. 5–16), and a concluding appeal (vv. 17–23), framed by the letter opening and the doxology. This is offered as a reading aid; Jude never names these categories.

The two analyses do not compete. A Jewish author writing in Greek could use both inherited Jewish methods and the persuasive patterns any educated speaker of Greek would know.

## 7. Jude's scriptural world

Jude is saturated with Israel's scriptures, yet he never introduces an Old Testament quotation with "it is written." His one formal quotation comes from 1 Enoch (vv. 14–15). His references to the Hebrew Bible are compressed allusions that assume the reader knows the story:

| Jude | Allusion |
|---|---|
| 5 | The exodus and the wilderness unbelief (Exod 12–14; Num 14) |
| 6 | The "sons of God" (Gen 6:1–4) as read in 1 Enoch 6–16 |
| 7 | Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19) |
| 9 | Michael and Moses' burial (Deut 34:5–6) via later tradition; Michael’s words echo Zech 3:2 ("YHWH pushes against you, O Satan") |
| 11 | Cain (Gen 4), Balaam (Num 22–24; 31:16), Korah (Num 16) |
| 12 | Shepherds feeding themselves (Ezek 34:2); clouds and wind without rain (Prov 25:14) |
| 13 | The restless sea casting up mire (Isa 57:20) |
| 14–15 | Enoch (Gen 5:21–24); 1 Enoch 1:9 |
| 16 | The wilderness grumbling (Exod 16; Num 14) |
| 23 | A brand snatched from the fire; filthy garments (Zech 3:2–4; Amos 4:11) |

One detail suggests that Jude knew his scriptures in Hebrew or Aramaic rather than only in the Greek Septuagint. In [Isa 57:20](#hl-hist-isa-57) and [Prov 25:14](#hl-hist-pro-25), the passages behind his images of the foaming sea and the rainless clouds, the Hebrew text contains the very details Jude uses: the sea "casts out filth and mire," and there are "clouds and wind without rain" (LSV, translating the Hebrew). The Septuagint versions of both verses lack those details.[^i-8] This is not proof, but it fits a Palestinian Jewish author.

Jude also draws on **Jewish traditions outside the Hebrew Bible**: 1 Enoch, the fullest surviving source for the Watcher story and for the prophecy he quotes, and a tradition about Michael's dispute with the Devil over Moses' body, which early Christian writers associated with a work called the *Assumption* (or *Ascension*) *of Moses*. These references were the main reason some early Christians hesitated over Jude. They are discussed fully in Chapters 3, 4, and 8.

## 8. Jude and 2 Peter

Anyone who reads Jude and then 2 Peter 2 notices the resemblance. The same sequence of themes and images appears in both: intruders who deny the Master (Jude 4; [2 Pet 2:1](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), sinning angels kept in gloom for judgment (Jude 6; [2 Pet 2:4](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), Sodom and Gomorrah (Jude 7; [2 Pet 2:6](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), defiling the flesh and despising authority (Jude 8; [2 Pet 2:10](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), angels who do not bring a slanderous judgment (Jude 9; [2 Pet 2:11](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), creatures without reason (Jude 10; [2 Pet 2:12](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), Balaam's love of reward (Jude 11; [2 Pet 2:15](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), feasting together (Jude 12; [2 Pet 2:13](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), waterless clouds and gloom of darkness (Jude 12–13; [2 Pet 2:17](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), "swollen" words (Jude 16; [2 Pet 2:18](#hl-hist-2pe-2)), and scoffers foretold by the apostles (Jude 17–18; [2 Pet 3:2–3](#hl-hist-2pe-3)). Three Greek words occur in the New Testament only in these two letters.

There are three main explanations:

1. **2 Peter used Jude.** Most modern scholars hold this view.[^i-8b] Jude's version is usually the more compact and more Jewish, and it is easier to explain why 2 Peter would omit Jude's quotation from Enoch and his named Michael story than why Jude would add them. 2 Peter also arranges the examples in biblical order (angels, flood, Sodom), while Jude's order follows his own thematic logic.
2. **Jude used 2 Peter.** This was Martin Luther's opinion. He wrote that Jude "refers to the second Epistle of St. Peter, from which it has taken nearly all its words." Some later scholars agreed, among them F. Spitta, as Mayor reports.[^i-8c] This view points to 2 Peter's future tense ("there will be false teachers," [2 Pet 2:1](#hl-hist-2pe-2)) and Jude's past tense ("there came in," Jude 4), as if Jude were reporting the fulfillment of 2 Peter's prediction.
3. **Both used a common source**, perhaps a body of early Christian teaching about false teachers.

Alfred Plummer, who weighed the question carefully in 1891, admitted that he "remains still uncertain as to the true relation between the two, and that he has inclined sometimes to the one, and sometimes to the other."[^i-8d] That honest uncertainty is a good guide.

The question matters for the study of 2 Peter more than for Jude. This book reads Jude on its own terms and uses 2 Peter as an early interpreter of Jude's language. Appendix C gives the parallel texts side by side.

## 9. How the church received Jude

Jude's place in the New Testament was secure early in some regions and debated in others, and the debate centered on his use of Enoch.

- **Late second century:** the Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list of accepted books whose date is debated, includes "the Epistle of Jude."[^i-9] Clement of Alexandria commented on Jude in his *Hypotyposes*, and part of that commentary survives in Latin.[^i-10] Tertullian, around AD 200, used Jude to defend Enoch's authority: "Enoch possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude."[^i-11]
- **Third century:** Origen praised Jude as "a letter of few lines, it is true, but filled with the healthful words of heavenly grace."[^i-12]
- **Early fourth century:** Eusebius placed Jude among the "disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many," noting that "not many of the ancients have mentioned it" but that it had been "read publicly in very many churches."[^i-13]
- **AD 367:** Athanasius's Easter letter listing the books of the New Testament includes "one of Jude" among the seven catholic epistles.[^i-14]
- **Late fourth century:** Jerome explained the hesitation directly: "because in it he quotes from the apocryphal Book of Enoch it is rejected by many. Nevertheless by age and use it has gained authority and is reckoned among the Holy Scriptures."[^i-15]

At the Reformation, Martin Luther judged in his 1523 sermons on Jude that the letter "cannot be looked upon as being that of one who was truly an Apostle, for the author speaks in it of the Apostles, as being much their junior," and that it "refers to the second Epistle of St. Peter, from which it has taken nearly all its words."[^i-16] John Calvin defended its authority and suggested that Jude drew on ancient tradition, not necessarily on an apocryphal book.[^i-17]

One further fact helps modern readers understand the issue. **The Book of Enoch, which Jude quotes, is itself part of the Old Testament canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church**, though not of other churches or of Judaism.[^i-18] The question "What does it mean that Jude quotes Enoch?" therefore receives different answers in different Christian traditions. Chapter 8 explores it.

## 10. Why Jude matters

Jude has been called the most neglected book of the New Testament. Its neglect is understandable but costly. In twenty-five verses it offers:

- a picture of **Christian identity** as gift before task: called, loved, kept;
- a clear statement that the **gospel has content**, entrusted once for all and worth contending for;
- an unflinching moral seriousness about **grace twisted into license**;
- a demonstration of how the first Christians read **Israel's scriptures and traditions** as speaking to their present;
- a remarkably early and high **Christology**: Jesus is "our only Master and Lord," possibly the one who saved Israel from Egypt, and the coming Lord of Enoch's prophecy;
- a model of **contending without contempt**, defending the faith while showing mercy to the wavering and rescuing those in danger;
- one of the most beautiful **doxologies** in Scripture, which turns the whole letter toward the God who keeps his people.

The chapters that follow try to show how these pieces fit together.

אֶת־יָבָל הוּא הָיָה אֲבִי יֹשֵׁב אֹהֶל וּמִקְנֶה **21** וְשֵׁם אָחִיו יוּבָל הוּא הָיָה אֲבִי כָּל־תֹּפֵשׂ כִּנּוֹר וְעוּגָב **22** וְצִלָּה גַם־הִוא יָלְדָה אֶת־תּוּבַל קַיִן לֹטֵשׁ כָּל־חֹרֵשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת וּבַרְזֶל וַאֲחוֹת תּוּבַל־קַיִן נַעֲמָה **23** וַיֹּאמֶר לֶמֶךְ לְנָשָׁיו עָדָה וְצִלָּה שְׁמַעַן קוֹלִי נְשֵׁי לֶמֶךְ הַאְזֵנָּה אִמְרָתִי כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי וְיֶלֶד לְחַבֻּרָתִי **24** כִּי שִׁבְעָתַיִם יֻקַּם־קָיִן וְלֶמֶךְ שִׁבְעִים וְשִׁבְעָה **25** וַיֵּדַע אָדָם עוֹד אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן וַתִּקְרָא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ שֵׁת כִּי שָׁת־לִי אֱלֹהִים זֶרַע אַחֵר תַּחַת הֶבֶל כִּי הֲרָגוֹ קָיִן **26** וּלְשֵׁת גַּם־הוּא יֻלַּד־בֵּן וַיִּקְרָא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ אֱנוֹשׁ אָז הוּחַל לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה
:::

*English (BSB)*

**1** And Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. “With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man,” she said. **2** Later she gave birth to Cain’s brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, while Cain was a tiller of the soil. **3** So in the course of time, Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil as an offering to the LORD, **4** while Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. And the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, **5** but He had no regard for Cain and his offering. So Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell. **6** “Why are you angry,” said the LORD to Cain, “and why has your countenance fallen? **7** If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.” **8** Then Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.” And while they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him. **9** And the LORD said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” “I do not know!” he answered. “Am I my brother’s keeper?” **10** “What have you done?” replied the LORD. “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground. **11** Now you are cursed and banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. **12** When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” **13** But Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is greater than I can bear. **14** Behold, this day You have driven me from the face of the earth, and from Your face I will be hidden; I will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me.” **15** “Not so!” replied the LORD. “If anyone slays Cain, then Cain will be avenged sevenfold.” And the LORD placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. **16** So Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. **17** And Cain had relations with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. Then Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch. **18** Now to Enoch was born Irad, and Irad was the father of Mehujael, and Mehujael was the father of Methusael, and Methusael was the father of Lamech. **19** And Lamech married two women, one named Adah and the other Zillah. **20** Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock. **21** And his brother’s name was Jubal; he was the father of all who play the harp and flute. **22** And Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah. **23** Then Lamech said to his wives: “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to my speech. For I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. **24** If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” **25** And Adam again had relations with his wife, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” **26** And to Seth also a son was born, and he called him Enosh. At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.

*English (WEB)*

**1** The man knew Eve his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Cain, and said, “I have gotten a man with the LORD’s help.” **2** Again she gave birth, to Cain’s brother Abel. Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. **3** As time passed, Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground. **4** Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. The LORD respected Abel and his offering, **5** but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell. **6** The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? **7** If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” **8** Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him. **9** The LORD said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” **10** The LORD said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground. **11** Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. **12** From now on, when you till the ground, it won’t yield its strength to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” **13** Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is greater than I can bear. **14** Behold, you have driven me out today from the surface of the ground. I will be hidden from your face, and I will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth. Whoever finds me will kill me.” **15** The LORD said to him, “Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.” The LORD appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him. **16** Cain left the LORD’s presence, and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden. **17** Cain knew his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Enoch. He built a city, and named the city after the name of his son, Enoch. **18** Irad was born to Enoch. Irad became the father of Mehujael. Mehujael became the father of Methushael. Methushael became the father of Lamech. **19** Lamech took two wives: the name of the first one was Adah, and the name of the second one was Zillah. **20** Adah gave birth to Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. **21** His brother’s name was Jubal, who was the father of all who handle the harp and pipe. **22** Zillah also gave birth to Tubal Cain, the forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron. Tubal Cain’s sister was Naamah. **23** Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice. You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech, for I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for bruising me. **24** If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.” **25** Adam knew his wife again. She gave birth to a son, and named him Seth, saying, “for God has given me another child instead of Abel, for Cain killed him.” **26** A son was also born to Seth, and he named him Enosh. At that time men began to call on the LORD’s name.

### Genesis 5:21–24 {#hl-hist-gen-5}

*Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)*

::: {lang=he dir=rtl}
**21** וַיְחִי חֲנוֹךְ חָמֵשׁ וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד אֶת־מְתוּשָׁלַח **22** וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת־מְתוּשֶׁלַח שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת **23** וַיְהִי כָּל־יְמֵי חֲנוֹךְ חָמֵשׁ וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה **24** וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֵינֶנּוּ כִּי־לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים
:::

*English (BSB)*

**21** When Enoch was 65 years old, he became the father of Methuselah. **22** And after he had become the father of Methuselah, Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters. **23** So Enoch lived a total of 365 years. **24** Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.

*English (WEB)*

**21** Enoch lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Methuselah. **22** After Methuselah’s birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and became the father of more sons and daughters. **23** All the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years. **24** Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.

### Genesis 6:1–4 {#hl-hist-gen-6}

*Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)*

Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown.

### Genesis 19 {#hl-hist-gen-19}

*Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)*

::: {lang=he dir=rtl}
**1** וַיָּבֹאוּ שְׁנֵי הַמַּלְאָכִים סְדֹמָה בָּעֶרֶב וְלוֹט יֹשֵׁב בְּשַׁעַר־סְדֹם וַיַּרְא־לוֹט וַיָּקָם לִקְרָאתָם וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ אַפַּיִם אָרְצָה **2** וַיֹּאמֶר הִנֶּה נָּא־אֲדֹנַי סוּרוּ נָא אֶל־בֵּית עַבְדְּכֶם וְלִינוּ וְרַחֲצוּ רַגְלֵיכֶם וְהִשְׁכַּמְתֶּם וַהֲלַכְתֶּם לְדַרְכְּכֶם וַיֹּאמְרוּ לֹּא כִּי בָרְחוֹב נָלִין **3** וַיִּפְצַר־בָּם מְאֹד וַיָּסֻרוּ אֵלָיו וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל־בֵּיתוֹ וַיַּעַשׂ לָהֶם מִשְׁתֶּה וּמַצּוֹת אָפָה וַיֹּאכֵלוּ **4** טֶרֶם יִשְׁכָּבוּ וְאַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר אַנְשֵׁי סְדֹם נָסַבּוּ עַל־הַבַּיִת מִנַּעַר וְעַד־זָקֵן כָּל־הָעָם מִקָּצֶה **5** וַיִּקְרְאוּ אֶל־לוֹט וַיֹּאמְרוּ לוֹ אַיֵּה הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר־בָּאוּ אֵלֶיךָ הַלָּיְלָה הוֹצִיאֵם אֵלֵינוּ וְנֵדְעָה אֹתָם **6** וַיֵּצֵא אֲלֵהֶם לוֹט הַפֶּתְחָה וְהַדֶּלֶת סָגַר אַחֲרָיו **7** וַיֹּאמַר אַל־נָא אַחַי תָּרֵעוּ **8** הִנֵּה־נָא לִי שְׁתֵּי בָנוֹת אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ אִישׁ אוֹצִיאָה־נָּא אֶתְהֶן אֲלֵיכֶם וַעֲשׂוּ לָהֶן כַּטּוֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶם רַק לָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵל אַל־תַּעֲשׂוּ דָבָר כִּי־עַל־כֵּן בָּאוּ בְּצֵל קֹרָתִי **9** וַיֹּאמְרוּ גֶּשׁ־הָלְאָה וַיֹּאמְרוּ הָאֶחָד בָּא־לָגוּר וַיִּשְׁפֹּט שָׁפוֹט עַתָּה נָרַע לְךָ מֵהֶם וַיִּפְצְרוּ בָאִישׁ בְּלוֹט מְאֹד וַיִּגְּשׁוּ לִשְׁבֹּר הַדָּלֶת **10** וַיִּשְׁלְחוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים אֶת־יָדָם וַיָּבִיאוּ אֶת־לוֹט אֲלֵיהֶם הַבָּיְתָה וְאֶת־הַדֶּלֶת סָגָרוּ **11** וְאֶת־הָאֲנָשִׁים אֲשֶׁר־פֶּתַח הַבַּיִת הִכּוּ בַּסַּנְוֵרִים מִקָּטֹן וְעַד־גָּדוֹל וַיִּלְאוּ לִמְצֹא הַפָּתַח **12** וַיֹּאמְרוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים אֶל־לוֹט עֹד מִי־לְךָ פֹה חָתָן וּבָנֶיךָ וּבְנֹתֶיךָ וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר־לְךָ בָּעִיר הוֹצֵא מִן־הַמָּקוֹם **13** כִּי־מַשְׁחִתִים אֲנַחְנוּ אֶת־הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה כִּי־גָדְלָה צַעֲקָתָם אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה וַיְשַׁלְּחֵנוּ יְהוָה לְשַׁחֲתָהּ **14** וַיֵּצֵא לוֹט וַיְדַבֵּר אֶל־חֲתָנָיו לֹקְחֵי בְנֹתָיו וַיֹּאמֶר קוּמוּ צְּאוּ מִן־הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה כִּי־מַשְׁחִית יְהוָה אֶת־הָעִיר וַיְהִי כִמְצַחֵק בְּעֵינֵי חֲתָנָיו **15** וּכְמוֹ הַשַּׁחַר עָלָה וַיָּאִיצוּ הַמַּלְאָכִים בְּלוֹט לֵאמֹר קוּם קַח אֶת־אִשְׁתְּךָ וְאֶת־שְׁתֵּי בְנֹתֶיךָ הַנִּמְצָאֹת פֶּן־תִּסָּפֶה בַּעֲוֺן הָעִיר **16** וַיִּתְמַהְמָהּ וַיַּחֲזִקוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים בְּיָדוֹ וּבְיַד־אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבְיַד שְׁתֵּי בְנֹתָיו בְּחֶמְלַת יְהוָה עָלָיו וַיֹּצִאֻהוּ וַיַּנִּחֻהוּ מִחוּץ לָעִיר **17** וַיְהִי כְהוֹצִיאָם אֹתָם הַחוּצָה וַיֹּאמֶר הִמָּלֵט עַל־נַפְשֶׁךָ אַל־תַּבִּיט אַחֲרֶיךָ וְאַל־תַּעֲמֹד בְּכָל־הַכִּכָּר הָהָרָה הִמָּלֵט פֶּן־תִּסָּפֶה **18** וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹט אֲלֵהֶם אַל־נָא אֲדֹנָי **19** הִנֵּה־נָא מָצָא עַבְדְּךָ חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ וַתַּגְדֵּל חַסְדְּךָ אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתָ עִמָּדִי לְהַחֲיוֹת אֶת־נַפְשִׁי וְאָנֹכִי לֹא אוּכַל לְהִמָּלֵט הָהָרָה פֶּן־תִּדְבָּקַנִי הָרָעָה וָמַתִּי **20** הִנֵּה־נָא הָעִיר הַזֹּאת קְרֹבָה לָנוּס שָׁמָּה וְהִיא מִצְעָר אִמָּלְטָה נָּא שָׁמָּה הֲלֹא מִצְעָר הִוא וּתְחִי נַפְשִׁי **21** וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו הִנֵּה נָשָׂאתִי פָנֶיךָ גַּם לַדָּבָר הַזֶּה לְבִלְתִּי הָפְכִּי אֶת־הָעִיר אֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתָּ **22** מַהֵר הִמָּלֵט שָׁמָּה כִּי לֹא אוּכַל לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר עַד־בֹּאֲךָ שָׁמָּה עַל־כֵּן קָרָא שֵׁם־הָעִיר צוֹעַר **23** הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ יָצָא עַל־הָאָרֶץ וְלוֹט בָּא צֹעֲרָה **24** וַיהוָה הִמְטִיר עַל־סְדֹם וְעַל־עֲמֹרָה גָּפְרִית וָאֵשׁ מֵאֵת יְהוָה מִן־הַשָּׁמָיִם **25** וַיַּהֲפֹךְ אֶת־הֶעָרִים הָאֵל וְאֵת כָּל־הַכִּכָּר וְאֵת כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵי הֶעָרִים וְצֶמַח הָאֲדָמָה **26** וַתַּבֵּט אִשְׁתּוֹ מֵאַחֲרָיו וַתְּהִי נְצִיב מֶלַח **27** וַיַּשְׁכֵּם אַבְרָהָם בַּבֹּקֶר אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר־עָמַד שָׁם אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה **28** וַיַּשְׁקֵף עַל־פְּנֵי סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה וְעַל־כָּל־פְּנֵי אֶרֶץ הַכִּכָּר וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה עָלָה קִיטֹר הָאָרֶץ כְּקִיטֹר הַכִּבְשָׁן **29** וַיְהִי בְּשַׁחֵת אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עָרֵי הַכִּכָּר וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־אַבְרָהָם וַיְשַׁלַּח אֶת־לוֹט מִתּוֹךְ הַהֲפֵכָה בַּהֲפֹךְ אֶת־הֶעָרִים אֲשֶׁר־יָשַׁב בָּהֵן לוֹט **30** וַיַּעַל לוֹט מִצּוֹעַר וַיֵּשֶׁב בָּהָר וּשְׁתֵּי בְנֹתָיו עִמּוֹ כִּי יָרֵא לָשֶׁבֶת בְּצוֹעַר וַיֵּשֶׁב בַּמְּעָרָה הוּא וּשְׁתֵּי בְנֹתָיו **31** וַתֹּאמֶר הַבְּכִירָה אֶל־הַצְּעִירָה אָבִינוּ זָקֵן וְאִישׁ אֵין בָּאָרֶץ לָבוֹא עָלֵינוּ כְּדֶרֶךְ כָּל־הָאָרֶץ **32** לְכָה נַשְׁקֶה אֶת־אָבִינוּ יַיִן וְנִשְׁכְּבָה עִמּוֹ וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע **33** וַתַּשְׁקֶיןָ אֶת־אֲבִיהֶן יַיִן בַּלַּיְלָה הוּא וַתָּבֹא הַבְּכִירָה וַתִּשְׁכַּב אֶת־אָבִיהָ וְלֹא־יָדַע בְּשִׁכְבָהּ וּבְקׄוּמָהּ **34** וַיְהִי מִמָּחֳרָת וַתֹּאמֶר הַבְּכִירָה אֶל־הַצְּעִירָה הֵן־שָׁכַבְתִּי אֶמֶשׁ אֶת־אָבִי נַשְׁקֶנּוּ יַיִן גַּם־הַלַּיְלָה וּבֹאִי שִׁכְבִי עִמּוֹ וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע **35** וַתַּשְׁקֶיןָ גַּם בַּלַּיְלָה הַהוּא אֶת־אֲבִיהֶן יָיִן וַתָּקָם הַצְּעִירָה וַתִּשְׁכַּב עִמּוֹ וְלֹא־יָדַע בְּשִׁכְבָהּ וּבְקֻמָהּ **36** וַתַּהֲרֶיןָ שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹת־לוֹט מֵאֲבִיהֶן **37** וַתֵּלֶד הַבְּכִירָה בֵּן וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ מוֹאָב הוּא אֲבִי־מוֹאָב עַד־הַיּוֹם **38** וְהַצְּעִירָה גַם־הִוא יָלְדָה בֵּן וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־עַמִּי הוּא אֲבִי בְנֵי־עַמּוֹן עַד־הַיּוֹם
:::

*English (BSB)*

**1** Now the two angels arrived at Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gateway of the city. When Lot saw them, he got up to meet them, bowed facedown, **2** and said, “My lords, please turn aside into the house of your servant; wash your feet and spend the night. Then you can rise early and go on your way.” “No,” they answered, “we will spend the night in the square.” **3** But Lot insisted so strongly that they followed him into his house. He prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate. **4** Before they had gone to bed, all the men of the city of Sodom, both young and old, surrounded the house. **5** They called out to Lot, saying, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Send them out to us so we can have relations with them!” **6** Lot went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him. **7** “Please, my brothers,” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing! **8** Look, I have two daughters who have never slept with a man. Let me bring them to you, and you can do to them as you please. But do not do anything to these men, for they have come under the protection of my roof.” **9** “Get out of the way!” they replied. And they declared, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge! Now we will treat you worse than them.” And they pressed in on Lot and moved in to break down the door. **10** But the men inside reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door. **11** And they struck the men at the entrance, young and old, with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door. **12** Then the two men said to Lot, “Do you have anyone else here—a son-in-law, your sons or daughters, or anyone else in the city who belongs to you? Get them out of here, **13** because we are about to destroy this place. For the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent us to destroy it.” **14** So Lot went out and spoke to the sons-in-law who were pledged in marriage to his daughters. “Get up,” he said. “Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city!” But his sons-in-law thought he was joking. **15** At daybreak the angels hurried Lot along, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away in the punishment of the city.” **16** But when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters. And they led them safely out of the city, because of the LORD’s compassion for them. **17** As soon as the men had brought them out, one of them said, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain! Flee to the mountains, or you will be swept away!” **18** But Lot replied, “No, my lords, please! **19** Your servant has indeed found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness by sparing my life. But I cannot run to the mountains; the disaster will overtake me, and I will die. **20** Look, there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place. Please let me flee there—is it not a small place? Then my life will be saved.” **21** “Very well,” he answered, “I will grant this request as well, and will not demolish the town you indicate. **22** Hurry! Run there quickly, for I cannot do anything until you reach it.” That is why the town was called Zoar. **23** And by the time the sun had risen over the land, Lot had reached Zoar. **24** Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah—from the LORD out of the heavens. **25** Thus He destroyed these cities and the entire plain, including all the inhabitants of the cities and everything that grew on the ground. **26** But Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt. **27** Early the next morning, Abraham got up and returned to the place where he had stood before the LORD. **28** He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and he saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace. **29** So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived. **30** Lot and his two daughters left Zoar and settled in the mountains—for he was afraid to stay in Zoar—where they lived in a cave. **31** One day the older daughter said to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to sleep with us, as is the custom over all the earth. **32** Come, let us get our father drunk with wine so we can sleep with him and preserve his line.” **33** So that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the firstborn went in and slept with her father; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up. **34** The next day the older daughter said to the younger, “Look, I slept with my father last night. Let us get him drunk with wine again tonight so you can go in and sleep with him and we can preserve our father’s line.” **35** So again that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the younger daughter went in and slept with him; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up. **36** Thus both of Lot’s daughters became pregnant by their father. **37** The older daughter gave birth to a son and named him Moab. He is the father of the Moabites of today. **38** The younger daughter also gave birth to a son, and she named him Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites of today.

*English (WEB)*

**1** The two angels came to Sodom at evening. Lot sat in the gate of Sodom. Lot saw them, and rose up to meet them. He bowed himself with his face to the earth, **2** and he said, “See now, my lords, please come into your servant’s house, stay all night, wash your feet, and you can rise up early, and go on your way.” They said, “No, but we will stay in the street all night.” **3** He urged them greatly, and they came in with him, and entered into his house. He made them a feast, and baked unleavened bread, and they ate. **4** But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, both young and old, all the people from every quarter. **5** They called to Lot, and said to him, “Where are the men who came in to you this night? Bring them out to us, that we may have sex with them.” **6** Lot went out to them through the door, and shut the door after himself. **7** He said, “Please, my brothers, don’t act so wickedly. **8** See now, I have two virgin daughters. Please let me bring them out to you, and you may do to them what seems good to you. Only don’t do anything to these men, because they have come under the shadow of my roof.” **9** They said, “Stand back!” Then they said, “This one fellow came in to live as a foreigner, and he appoints himself a judge. Now we will deal worse with you than with them!” They pressed hard on the man Lot, and came near to break the door. **10** But the men reached out their hand, and brought Lot into the house to them, and shut the door. **11** They struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great, so that they wearied themselves to find the door. **12** The men said to Lot, “Do you have anybody else here? Sons-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and whomever you have in the city, bring them out of the place: **13** for we will destroy this place, because the outcry against them has grown so great before the LORD that the LORD has sent us to destroy it.” **14** Lot went out, and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were pledged to marry his daughters, and said, “Get up! Get out of this place, for the LORD will destroy the city!” But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be joking. **15** When the morning came, then the angels hurried Lot, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.” **16** But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, the LORD being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city. **17** It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!” **18** Lot said to them, “Oh, not so, my lord. **19** See now, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have magnified your loving kindness, which you have shown to me in saving my life. I can’t escape to the mountain, lest evil overtake me, and I die. **20** See now, this city is near to flee to, and it is a little one. Oh let me escape there (isn’t it a little one?), and my soul will live.” **21** He said to him, “Behold, I have granted your request concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken. **22** Hurry, escape there, for I can’t do anything until you get there.” Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar. **23** The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar. **24** Then the LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of the sky. **25** He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground. **26** But Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt. **27** Abraham went up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD. **28** He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and saw that the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace. **29** When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot lived. **30** Lot went up out of Zoar, and lived in the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he was afraid to live in Zoar. He lived in a cave with his two daughters. **31** The firstborn said to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is not a man on the earth to come in to us in the way of all the earth. **32** Come, let’s make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve our father’s family line.” **33** They made their father drink wine that night: and the firstborn went in, and lay with her father. He didn’t know when she lay down, nor when she arose. **34** It came to pass on the next day, that the firstborn said to the younger, “Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let’s make him drink wine again tonight. You go in, and lie with him, that we may preserve our father’s family line.” **35** They made their father drink wine that night also. The younger went and lay with him. He didn’t know when she lay down, nor when she got up. **36** Thus both of Lot’s daughters were with child by their father. **37** The firstborn bore a son, and named him Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. **38** The younger also bore a son, and called his name Ben Ammi. He is the father of the children of Ammon to this day.

### Exodus 12 {#hl-hist-exo-12}

*Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)*

::: {lang=he dir=rtl}
**1** וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל־מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל־אַהֲרֹן בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם לֵאמֹר **2** הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם רֹאשׁ חֳדָשִׁים רִאשׁוֹן הוּא לָכֶם לְחָדְשֵׁי הַשָּׁנָה **3** דַּבְּרוּ אֶל־כָּל־עֲדַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר בֶּעָשֹׂר לַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה וְיִקְחוּ לָהֶם אִישׁ שֶׂה לְבֵית־אָבֹת שֶׂה לַבָּיִת **4** וְאִם־יִמְעַט הַבַּיִת מִהְיֹת מִשֶּׂה וְלָקַח הוּא וּשְׁכֵנוֹ הַקָּרֹב אֶל־בֵּיתוֹ בְּמִכְסַת נְפָשֹׁת אִישׁ לְפִי אָכְלוֹ תָּכֹסּוּ עַל־הַשֶּׂה **5** שֶׂה תָמִים זָכָר בֶּן־שָׁנָה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם מִן־הַכְּבָשִׂים וּמִן־הָעִזִּים תִּקָּחוּ **6** וְהָיָה לָכֶם לְמִשְׁמֶרֶת עַד אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה וְשָׁחֲטוּ אֹתוֹ כֹּל קְהַל עֲדַת־יִשְׂרָאֵל בֵּין הָעַרְבָּיִם **7** וְלָקְחוּ מִן־הַדָּם וְנָתְנוּ עַל־שְׁתֵּי הַמְּזוּזֹת וְעַל־הַמַּשְׁקוֹף עַל הַבָּתִּים אֲשֶׁר־יֹאכְלוּ אֹתוֹ בָּהֶם **8** וְאָכְלוּ אֶת־הַבָּשָׂר בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה צְלִי־אֵשׁ וּמַצּוֹת עַל־מְרֹרִים יֹאכְלֻהוּ **9** אַל־תֹּאכְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ נָא וּבָשֵׁל מְבֻשָּׁל בַּמָּיִם כִּי אִם־צְלִי־אֵשׁ רֹאשׁוֹ עַל־כְּרָעָיו וְעַל־קִרְבּוֹ **10** וְלֹא־תוֹתִירוּ מִמֶּנּוּ עַד־בֹּקֶר וְהַנֹּתָר מִמֶּנּוּ עַד־בֹּקֶר בָּאֵשׁ תִּשְׂרֹפוּ **11** וְכָכָה תֹּאכְלוּ אֹתוֹ מָתְנֵיכֶם חֲגֻרִים נַעֲלֵיכֶם בְּרַגְלֵיכֶם וּמַקֶּלְכֶם בְּיֶדְכֶם וַאֲכַלְתֶּם אֹתוֹ בְּחִפָּזוֹן פֶּסַח הוּא לַיהוָה **12** וְעָבַרְתִּי בְאֶרֶץ־מִצְרַיִם בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה וְהִכֵּיתִי כָל־בְּכוֹר בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מֵאָדָם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה וּבְכָל־אֱלֹהֵי מִצְרַיִם אֶעֱשֶׂה שְׁפָטִים אֲנִי יְהוָה **13** וְהָיָה הַדָּם לָכֶם לְאֹת עַל הַבָּתִּים אֲשֶׁר אַתֶּם שָׁם וְרָאִיתִי אֶת־הַדָּם וּפָסַחְתִּי עֲלֵכֶם וְלֹא־יִהְיֶה בָכֶם נֶגֶף לְמַשְׁחִית בְּהַכֹּתִי בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם **14** וְהָיָה הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה לָכֶם לְזִכָּרוֹן וְחַגֹּתֶם אֹתוֹ חַג לַיהוָה לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם חֻקַּת עוֹלָם תְּחָגֻּהוּ **15** שִׁבְעַת יָמִים מַצּוֹת תֹּאכֵלוּ אַךְ בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן תַּשְׁבִּיתוּ שְּׂאֹר מִבָּתֵּיכֶם כִּי כָּל־אֹכֵל חָמֵץ וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל מִיּוֹם הָרִאשֹׁן עַד־יוֹם הַשְּׁבִעִי **16** וּבַיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן מִקְרָא־קֹדֶשׁ וּבַיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי מִקְרָא־קֹדֶשׁ יִהְיֶה לָכֶם כָּל־מְלָאכָה לֹא־יֵעָשֶׂה בָהֶם אַךְ אֲשֶׁר יֵאָכֵל לְכָל־נֶפֶשׁ הוּא לְבַדּוֹ יֵעָשֶׂה לָכֶם **17** וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת־הַמַּצּוֹת כִּי בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה הוֹצֵאתִי אֶת־צִבְאוֹתֵיכֶם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת־הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם חֻקַּת עוֹלָם **18** בָּרִאשֹׁן בְּאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ בָּעֶרֶב תֹּאכְלוּ מַצֹּת עַד יוֹם הָאֶחָד וְעֶשְׂרִים לַחֹדֶשׁ בָּעָרֶב **19** שִׁבְעַת יָמִים שְׂאֹר לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּבָתֵּיכֶם כִּי כָּל־אֹכֵל מַחְמֶצֶת וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא מֵעֲדַת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּגֵּר וּבְאֶזְרַח הָאָרֶץ **20** כָּל־מַחְמֶצֶת לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ בְּכֹל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם תֹּאכְלוּ מַצּוֹת **21** וַיִּקְרָא מֹשֶׁה לְכָל־זִקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם מִשְׁכוּ וּקְחוּ לָכֶם צֹאן לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתֵיכֶם וְשַׁחֲטוּ הַפָּסַח **22** וּלְקַחְתֶּם אֲגֻדַּת אֵזוֹב וּטְבַלְתֶּם בַּדָּם אֲשֶׁר־בַּסַּף וְהִגַּעְתֶּם אֶל־הַמַּשְׁקוֹף וְאֶל־שְׁתֵּי הַמְּזוּזֹת מִן־הַדָּם אֲשֶׁר בַּסָּף וְאַתֶּם לֹא תֵצְאוּ אִישׁ מִפֶּתַח־בֵּיתוֹ עַד־בֹּקֶר **23** וְעָבַר יְהוָה לִנְגֹּף אֶת־מִצְרַיִם וְרָאָה אֶת־הַדָּם עַל־הַמַּשְׁקוֹף וְעַל שְׁתֵּי הַמְּזוּזֹת וּפָסַח יְהוָה עַל־הַפֶּתַח וְלֹא יִתֵּן הַמַּשְׁחִית לָבֹא אֶל־בָּתֵּיכֶם לִנְגֹּף **24** וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה לְחָק־לְךָ וּלְבָנֶיךָ עַד־עוֹלָם **25** וְהָיָה כִּי־תָבֹאוּ אֶל־הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן יְהוָה לָכֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֵּר וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת־הָעֲבֹדָה הַזֹּאת **26** וְהָיָה כִּי־יֹאמְרוּ אֲלֵיכֶם בְּנֵיכֶם מָה הָעֲבֹדָה הַזֹּאת לָכֶם **27** וַאֲמַרְתֶּם זֶבַח־פֶּסַח הוּא לַיהוָה אֲשֶׁר פָּסַח עַל־בָּתֵּי בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמִצְרַיִם בְּנָגְפּוֹ אֶת־מִצְרַיִם וְאֶת־בָּתֵּינוּ הִצִּיל וַיִּקֹּד הָעָם וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲוּוּ **28** וַיֵּלְכוּ וַיַּעֲשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת־מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן כֵּן עָשׂוּ **29** וַיְהִי בַּחֲצִי הַלַּיְלָה וַיהוָה הִכָּה כָל־בְּכוֹר בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מִבְּכֹר פַּרְעֹה הַיֹּשֵׁב עַל־כִּסְאוֹ עַד בְּכוֹר הַשְּׁבִי אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵית הַבּוֹר וְכֹל בְּכוֹר בְּהֵמָה **30** וַיָּקָם פַּרְעֹה לַיְלָה הוּא וְכָל־עֲבָדָיו וְכָל־מִצְרַיִם וַתְּהִי צְעָקָה גְדֹלָה בְּמִצְרָיִם כִּי־אֵין בַּיִת אֲשֶׁר אֵין־שָׁם מֵת **31** וַיִּקְרָא לְמֹשֶׁה וּלְאַהֲרֹן לַיְלָה וַיֹּאמֶר קוּמוּ צְּאוּ מִתּוֹךְ עַמִּי גַּם־אַתֶּם גַּם־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְכוּ עִבְדוּ אֶת־יְהוָה כְּדַבֶּרְכֶם **32** גַּם־צֹאנְכֶם גַּם־בְּקַרְכֶם קְחוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתֶּם וָלֵכוּ וּבֵרַכְתֶּם גַּם־אֹתִי **33** וַתֶּחֱזַק מִצְרַיִם עַל־הָעָם לְמַהֵר לְשַׁלְּחָם מִן־הָאָרֶץ כִּי אָמְרוּ כֻּלָּנוּ מֵתִים **34** וַיִּשָּׂא הָעָם אֶת־בְּצֵקוֹ טֶרֶם יֶחְמָץ מִשְׁאֲרֹתָם צְרֻרֹת בְּשִׂמְלֹתָם עַל־שִׁכְמָם **35** וּבְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל עָשׂוּ כִּדְבַר מֹשֶׁה וַיִּשְׁאֲלוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם כְּלֵי־כֶסֶף וּכְלֵי זָהָב וּשְׂמָלֹת **36** וַיהוָה נָתַן אֶת־חֵן הָעָם בְּעֵינֵי מִצְרַיִם וַיַּשְׁאִלוּם וַיְנַצְּלוּ אֶת־מִצְרָיִם **37** וַיִּסְעוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵרַעְמְסֵס סֻכֹּתָה כְּשֵׁשׁ־מֵאוֹת אֶלֶף רַגְלִי הַגְּבָרִים לְבַד מִטָּף **38** וְגַם־עֵרֶב רַב עָלָה אִתָּם וְצֹאן וּבָקָר מִקְנֶה כָּבֵד מְאֹד **39** וַיֹּאפוּ אֶת־הַבָּצֵק אֲשֶׁר הוֹצִיאוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם עֻגֹת מַצּוֹת כִּי לֹא חָמֵץ כִּי־גֹרְשׁוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לְהִתְמַהְמֵהַּ וְגַם־צֵדָה לֹא־עָשׂוּ לָהֶם **40** וּמוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָשְׁבוּ בְּמִצְרָיִם שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה **41** וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיְהִי בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה יָצְאוּ כָּל־צִבְאוֹת יְהוָה מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם **42** לֵיל שִׁמֻּרִים הוּא לַיהוָה לְהוֹצִיאָם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם הוּא־הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה לַיהוָה שִׁמֻּרִים לְכָל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְדֹרֹתָם **43** וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל־מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן זֹאת חֻקַּת הַפָּסַח כָּל־בֶּן־נֵכָר לֹא־יֹאכַל בּוֹ **44** וְכָל־עֶבֶד אִישׁ מִקְנַת־כָּסֶף וּמַלְתָּה אֹתוֹ אָז יֹאכַל בּוֹ **45** תּוֹשָׁב וְשָׂכִיר לֹא־יֹאכַל־בּוֹ **46** בְּבַיִת אֶחָד יֵאָכֵל לֹא־תוֹצִיא מִן־הַבַּיִת מִן־הַבָּשָׂר חוּצָה וְעֶצֶם לֹא תִשְׁבְּרוּ־בוֹ **47** כָּל־עֲדַת יִשְׂרָאֵל יַעֲשׂוּ אֹתוֹ **48** וְכִי־יָגוּר אִתְּךָ גֵּר וְעָשָׂה פֶסַח לַיהוָה הִמּוֹל לוֹ כָל־זָכָר וְאָז יִקְרַב לַעֲשֹׂתוֹ וְהָיָה כְּאֶזְרַח הָאָרֶץ וְכָל־עָרֵל לֹא־יֹאכַל בּוֹ **49** תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָאֶזְרָח וְלַגֵּר הַגָּר בְּתוֹכְכֶם **50** וַיַּעֲשׂוּ כָּל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת־מֹשֶׁה וְאֶת־אַהֲרֹן כֵּן עָשׂוּ **51** וַיְהִי בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה הוֹצִיא יְהוָה אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם עַל־צִבְאֹתָם
:::

*English (BSB)*

**1** Now the LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, **2** “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year. **3** Tell the whole congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month each man must select a lamb for his family, one per household. **4** If the household is too small for a whole lamb, they are to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people, and apportion the lamb accordingly. **5** Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats. **6** You must keep it until the fourteenth day of the month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel will slaughter the animals at twilight. **7** They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. **8** They are to eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. **9** Do not eat any of the meat raw or cooked in boiling water, but only roasted over the fire—its head and legs and inner parts. **10** Do not leave any of it until morning; before the morning you must burn up any part that is left over. **11** This is how you are to eat it: You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover. **12** On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male, both man and beast, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD. **13** The blood on the houses where you are staying will distinguish them; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. **14** And this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come. **15** For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened from the first day through the seventh must be cut off from Israel. **16** On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly, and another on the seventh day. You must not do any work on those days, except to prepare the meals—that is all you may do. **17** So you are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt. You must keep this day as a permanent statute for the generations to come. **18** In the first month you are to eat unleavened bread, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day. **19** For seven days there must be no leaven found in your houses. If anyone eats something leavened, that person, whether a foreigner or native of the land, must be cut off from the congregation of Israel. **20** You are not to eat anything leavened; eat unleavened bread in all your homes.” **21** Then Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and told them, “Go at once and select for yourselves a lamb for each family, and slaughter the Passover lamb. **22** Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe. None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning. **23** When the LORD passes through to strike down the Egyptians, He will see the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe and will pass over that doorway; so He will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and strike you down. **24** And you are to keep this command as a permanent statute for you and your descendants. **25** When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service. **26** When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’ **27** you are to reply, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when He struck down the Egyptians and spared our homes.’” Then the people bowed down and worshiped. **28** And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. **29** Now at midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as all the firstborn among the livestock. **30** During the night Pharaoh got up—he and all his officials and all the Egyptians—and there was loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead. **31** Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. **32** Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart! And bless me also.” **33** And in order to send them out of the land quickly, the Egyptians urged the people on. “For otherwise,” they said, “we are all going to die!” **34** So the people took their dough before it was leavened, carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing. **35** Furthermore, the Israelites acted on Moses’ word and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. **36** And the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request. In this way they plundered the Egyptians. **37** The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth with about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. **38** And a mixed multitude also went up with them, along with great droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. **39** Since their dough had no leaven, the people baked what they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened loaves. For when they had been driven out of Egypt, they could not delay and had not prepared any provisions for themselves. **40** Now the duration of the Israelites’ stay in Egypt was 430 years. **41** At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt. **42** Because the LORD kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt, this same night is to be a vigil to the LORD, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come. **43** And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the statute of the Passover: No foreigner is to eat of it. **44** But any slave who has been purchased may eat of it, after you have circumcised him. **45** A temporary resident or hired hand shall not eat the Passover. **46** It must be eaten inside one house.
