## B. Plain-English Orientation

Jude completes his series of images with two more, drawn from the sea and the sky. The intruders are like **wild waves** that throw up foam and scum on the shore, except that what they throw up is their own shameful conduct. They are also like **wandering stars**, heavenly bodies that have left their proper courses and for whom the deepest darkness has been reserved forever.

Together with the clouds and trees of v. 12, these images complete a tour of the created world: the air, the earth, the sea, and the heavens. In each region Jude finds a picture of disorder: clouds that do not rain, trees that do not bear, waves that cannot rest, stars that do not keep their paths. Jewish readers familiar with 1 Enoch would have recognized the pattern. In the natural world, everything obeys God's order. Only sinners do not.

## C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

### κύματα ἄγρια θαλάσσης (*kymata agria thalassēs*) — ‘wild waves of the sea’

The Greek κύματα ἄγρια θαλάσσης (*kymata agria thalassēs*) means "wild waves of the sea." The adjective ἄγριος (*agrios*) is used of wild animals and uncultivated land. Here it describes the untamed, restless violence of a stormy sea.

For the people of the Bible, the sea was not a place of recreation. It was the great image of chaos and danger. In the beginning "darkness [was] on the face of the deep" ([Gen 1:2](#hl-c07-gen-1), LSV), and God's power is shown in setting limits to the sea: "Who has made sand the border of the sea, / A perpetual limit, and it does not pass over it, / They shake themselves, and they are not able" ([Jer 5:22](#hl-c07-jer-5), LSV). In Job, God says to the sea, "To here you come, and no more, / And a command is placed / On the pride of your billows" ([Job 38:11](#hl-c07-job-38), LSV). The Psalms praise God as "ruler over the pride of the sea" ([Ps 89:9](#hl-c07-psa-89), LSV). The sea is powerful, but in Scripture it is held in check by God's command.

### ἐπαφρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας (*epaphrizonta tas heautōn aischynas*) — ‘foaming up their own shameful deeds’

The participle ἐπαφρίζοντα (*epaphrizonta*), "foaming up," another word found only here in the New Testament, comes from ἀφρός (*aphros*), "foam."[^c7-1] The image is of breakers that heave up foam, weed, and debris and leave them on the shore.

What the waves throw up is τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας (*tas heautōn aischynas*), "their own shames," a plural meaning "shameful deeds" or "disgraceful things." The LSV supplies "[deeds]" to make the sense clear.

The image almost certainly draws on Isaiah: "And the wicked [are] as the driven out sea, / For it is not able to rest, / And its waters cast out filth and mire. 'There is no peace,' said my God, 'for the wicked!'" ([Isa 57:20–21](#hl-c07-isa-57), LSV). As noted in the Introduction, the Greek Septuagint version of this verse lacks the "filth and mire," while the Hebrew includes it. Jude's image matches the Hebrew.[^c7-2]

The point is twofold. First, the intruders are restless and agitated, never at peace, always churning, like the sea of Isaiah that "is not able to rest." Second, their activity produces only filth. As a storm leaves a beach strewn with foam and debris, their teaching and conduct leave behind visible shame. Paul's description of those "whose glory [is] in their shame" ([Phil 3:19](#hl-c07-php-3), LSV) is a close parallel. The intruders may have boasted of their freedom, but what they produced was disgraceful.

### ἀστέρες πλανῆται (*asteres planētai*) — ‘wandering stars’

The final image is ἀστέρες πλανῆται (*asteres planētai*), "wandering stars." The LSV's "stars going astray" brings out the moral sense of πλανάω (*planaō*), "to lead astray, wander." The noun πλανήτης (*planētēs*), "wanderer," unique in the New Testament to this verse, is the source of the English word "planet."[^c7-3] Greek astronomers called the planets "wandering stars" because, unlike the fixed stars, they moved across the sky along irregular-seeming paths. The word also links back to "the deceit (πλάνη, *planē*) of Balaam" in v. 11. The intruders wander, and they lead others to wander.

What did Jude's readers picture? Several possibilities have been suggested, and they are not mutually exclusive:

1. **Planets.** The ordinary meaning of the phrase. To an observer, the planets seemed to break the regular order of the heavens.
2. **Shooting stars or meteors.** Stars that appear to fall from their places and vanish into darkness. This fits "for whom the gloom of the darkness … has been kept," but the word πλανῆται does not usually mean meteors.
3. **Stars as angels.** In Jewish and early Christian thought, stars were often associated with angels ([Rev 1:20; 9:1](#hl-c07-rev-1); [Job 38:7](#hl-c07-job-38)). In 1 Enoch, as the deep dive shows, disobedient stars are punished in a place of darkness and fire. On this reading, the intruders are compared to the rebellious heavenly beings of v. 6.

The third possibility is the strongest, because of Jude's evident use of 1 Enoch. It combines naturally with the first. To an ancient Jewish observer, a "wandering" star might be precisely a star that had transgressed its appointed course.

There may also be a practical image here. Ancient sailors navigated by the stars. A star that did not keep its place would lead travelers astray, just as the intruders' teaching misled the community. That fits the nautical imagery of the reefs (v. 12) and the sea (v. 13).

### οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται (*hois ho zophos tou skotous eis aiōna tetērētai*) — ‘for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever’

The final clause, οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται (*hois ho zophos tou skotous eis aiōna tetērētai*), "for whom the gloom of darkness has been reserved forever," announces the destiny of the wandering stars. It repeats two key terms:

- **ζόφος** (*zophos*), "gloom," used in v. 6 for the darkness in which the rebellious angels are held. The repetition binds the intruders' fate to the angels'.
- **τετήρηται** (*tetērētai*), "has been kept," the perfect passive of τηρέω (*tēreō*). This is the fourth occurrence of "keep" in the letter. The readers have been kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1). The angels did not keep their position and are kept in bonds (v. 6). Now darkness is kept for the intruders.

The phrase "the gloom of the darkness" (ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους) doubles the idea of darkness, which is something like "the blackness of darkness" (WBS) or "blackest darkness" (BSB). The LSV's "throughout the age" renders εἰς αἰῶνα (*eis aiōna*), literally "into the age," a common biblical idiom for "forever." Some manuscripts read εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα with the article. The meaning is unchanged.[^c7-4]

For a star, whose nature is to shine, the ultimate judgment is darkness. The image recalls Jesus' sayings about "the outer darkness—there will be the weeping and the gnashing of the teeth" ([Matt 8:12](#hl-c07-mat-8), LSV). Second Peter uses Jude's phrase almost word for word: "to whom the deepest gloom of darkness has been kept throughout the age" ([2 Pet 2:17](#hl-c07-2pe-2), LSV).

## D. Original-Language Investigation

| Greek | Transliteration | Basic meaning | In context | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| κῦμα | *kyma* | wave | "waves" | |
| ἄγριος | *agrios* | wild, fierce | "wild" | Used of untamed animals. |
| θάλασσα | *thalassa* | sea | "a sea" | Biblical symbol of chaos restrained by God. |
| ἐπαφρίζω | *epaphrizō* | foam up | "foaming up" | NT hapax; from ἀφρός, foam. |
| αἰσχύνη | *aischynē* | shame, disgrace | "shameful [deeds]" | Plural: shameful acts. |
| ἀστήρ | *astēr* | star | "stars" | |
| πλανήτης | *planētēs* | wanderer | "going astray" | NT hapax; source of "planet"; cf. πλάνη (v. 11). |
| ζόφος | *zophos* | gloom, deep darkness | "the gloom" | Also v. 6. |
| σκότος | *skotos* | darkness | "the darkness" | |
| αἰών | *aiōn* | age; (εἰς αἰῶνα) forever | "throughout the age" | |
| τηρέω | *tēreō* | keep, reserve | "has been kept" | Perfect passive; fourth use in Jude. |

**A caution on "planet."** It is tempting to read modern astronomy into Jude's "wandering stars," as though Jude were making a scientific observation about planetary orbits. Jude uses the ancient observational category, lights in the sky that do not keep the regular pattern of the fixed stars, and gives it a moral and theological meaning. The image works because, to his readers, the heavens normally displayed perfect order.

### Deep dive: Wandering stars and ancient cosmological imagery

To understand Jude's last image, it helps to step into the ancient view of the heavens.

**Order in the heavens.** For ancient peoples, the night sky was the supreme picture of order. The fixed stars wheeled in the same patterns year after year, and the calendar, agriculture, and navigation depended on them. Scripture celebrates this order: "Praise Him, sun and moon, / Praise Him, all stars of light. … He gave a statute, and they do not pass over" ([Ps 148:3, 6](#hl-c07-psa-148), LSV). Jeremiah speaks of God as the one "giving the sun for a light by day, / The statutes of moon and stars for a light by night" ([Jer 31:35](#hl-c07-jer-31), LSV). The Jewish *Testament of Naphtali* draws the moral lesson: "Sun and moon and stars change not their order; so also you shall not change the law of God in the disorderliness of your doings."[^c7-5]

**Disorder as rebellion.** Against this background, a heavenly body that did not keep its course was a picture of rebellion. 1 Enoch develops this idea vividly. Enoch, on his heavenly journey, sees "seven stars like great burning mountains," and the angel explains: "This place is the end of heaven and earth: this has become a prison for the stars and the host of heaven. And the stars which roll over the fire are they which have transgressed the commandment of the Lord in the beginning of their rising, because they did not come forth at their appointed times. And He was wroth with them, and bound them" ([1 Enoch 18:13–16](#hl-c07-1en-18), trans. Charles).[^c7-6] Later he sees "seven stars of the heaven bound together," and is told: "These are of the number of the stars ⌈of heaven⌉, which have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and are bound here" (21:3, 6).

In 1 Enoch these stars are closely linked with the fallen angels. Their "prison" is described in the same terms as the angels' prison (21:10: "This place is the prison of the angels"). Clement of Alexandria read Jude 13 in this way: "Wandering stars,—that is, he means those who err and are apostates are of that kind of stars which fell from the seats of the angels—to whom, for their apostasy, the blackness of darkness is reserved forever."[^c7-7]

**The four regions of nature.** The pattern goes further. 1 Enoch opens, immediately after the prophecy Jude quotes in vv. 14–15, with a call to observe the obedience of nature:

> Observe ye everything that takes place in the heaven, how they do not change their orbits, ⌈and⌉ the luminaries which are in the heaven, how they all rise and set in order each in its season, and transgress not against their appointed order. … Behold the summer and the winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and clouds and dew and rain lie upon it.
>
> — [1 Enoch 2:1, 3](#hl-c07-1en-2) (trans. Charles)

It goes on to the trees ("how the trees cover themselves with green leaves and bear fruit," 5:1) and the sea ("how the sea and the rivers in like manner accomplish and change not their tasks," 5:3). Then it turns to the sinners: "But ye—ye have not been steadfast, nor done the commandments of the Lord, But ye have turned away and spoken proud and hard words With your impure mouths against His greatness" (5:4).[^c7-8]

Later, 1 Enoch describes how, "in the days of the sinners," nature itself will fall into disorder: "the rain shall be kept back," "the fruits of the trees shall be withheld in their time," and "many chiefs of the stars shall transgress the order (prescribed)" ([1 Enoch 80:2–3, 6](#hl-c07-1en-80)).[^c7-9]

Compare Jude's four nature images:

| Jude 12–13 | Region | 1 Enoch 2–5: obedient nature | 1 Enoch 80: disorder in the days of sinners |
|---|---|---|---|
| "waterless clouds" | air/sky | "clouds and dew and rain lie upon it" (2:3) | "the rain shall be kept back" (80:2) |
| "autumnal trees without fruit" | earth | "the trees … bear fruit" (5:1) | "the fruits of the trees shall be withheld" (80:3) |
| "wild waves of a sea" | sea | "the sea and the rivers … change not their tasks" (5:3) | — |
| "stars going astray" | heavens | luminaries "transgress not against their appointed order" (2:1) | "many chiefs of the stars shall transgress the order" (80:6) |

The correspondence is striking enough to suggest that Jude had these passages of 1 Enoch in mind. J. B. Mayor drew the same connection for the last image: "ἀστέρες πλανῆται. This is borrowed from Enoch," citing [1 Enoch 80](#hl-c07-1en-80), "In the days of the sinners, many chiefs of the stars will err, and will alter their orbits and tasks."[^c7-10] Each part of creation has its God-given task: clouds give rain, trees bear fruit, the sea keeps its bounds, and stars keep their courses. The intruders are like nature gone wrong. They fail their purpose as surely as a rainless cloud, a fruitless tree, a sea that will not rest, or a star that leaves its path.

The parallel also explains why Jude's images move straight into the quotation from Enoch (vv. 14–15). [1 Enoch 1:9](#hl-c07-1en-1), which Jude quotes, stands just before the call to "observe" nature in chapters 2–5. Jude may be moving through a passage he knew well: the nature contrast first, then the prophecy that precedes it in the book.

**What Jude adds.** Jude does not simply repeat 1 Enoch. He applies its cosmic images to people *within* the Christian community, which turns a description of the wicked in general into a warning about leaders the readers know. He also connects the stars' fate with the language of "keeping" that runs through his letter.

## E. The Historical and Cultural World

**The sea in the ancient Near East.** In the myths of Israel's neighbors, the sea was a chaotic divine power that the storm god had to defeat. Israel's scriptures echo this imagery but transform it. The sea is a creature, powerful but subject to the LORD ([Ps 93:3–4](#hl-c07-psa-93)). For people who lived mostly inland and knew the sea from the coastline or from dangerous voyages, its restless waves and debris-strewn beaches were familiar images of turmoil.

**Astronomy and astrology.** Educated people in the Greco-Roman world knew the five visible planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) as "wanderers." Many also believed that the stars and planets influenced human affairs, and astrology was widespread. Jewish and Christian writers generally rejected astrological fatalism. 1 Enoch even warns that sinners will "err and take them to be gods" (80:7). Jude uses the image of wandering stars to describe people who have left their place, not to say anything about the influence of the heavens.

**Darkness and judgment.** In both Jewish and Greek thought, the realm of the dead and the place of punishment were associated with darkness, ζόφος in Homer, "outer darkness" in Jesus' sayings, and the dark prison of the angels in 1 Enoch. Jude draws on this shared imagery.

## F. Connections Across Scripture

**[Isaiah 57:20–21](#hl-c07-isa-57) (probable allusion).** "The wicked [are] as the driven out sea, / For it is not able to rest, / And its waters cast out filth and mire" (LSV). Jude's image of waves foaming up shame matches the Hebrew of this verse closely.

**[Job 38:8–11](#hl-c07-job-38); [Psalm 89:9](#hl-c07-psa-89); [Jeremiah 5:22](#hl-c07-jer-5) (shared theme).** God's restraint of the sea's "pride" provides the background against which "wild waves" appear as rebellion.

**[James 1:6](#hl-c07-jas-1) (verbal and thematic link).** James compares "he who is doubting" to "a wave of the sea, driven by wind and tossed" (LSV). The verb translated "doubting" (διακρίνομαι, *diakrinomai*) is the same verb Jude uses of those who are "doubting" in v. 22. The restless sea is an image of instability both in James and in Jude.

**[Revelation 1:20; 8:10; 9:1](#hl-c07-rev-1); [Isaiah 14:12](#hl-c07-isa-14) (shared imagery).** Stars as angels, and fallen stars as images of judgment or of rebellious powers, appear across Scripture. Isaiah's taunt against the king of Babylon, "How you have fallen from the heavens, / O shining one, son of the dawn!" ([Isa 14:12](#hl-c07-isa-14), LSV), was later read by many Christian interpreters as a description of Satan's fall.

**[Daniel 12:3](#hl-c07-dan-12); Philippians 2:15 (contrast).** The faithful are pictured as stars that shine: "those justifying the multitude as stars for all time and forever" ([Dan 12:3](#hl-c07-dan-12), LSV); believers "appear as luminaries in the world" ([Phil 2:15](#hl-c07-php-2), LSV). The wandering stars of Jude 13 are their dark opposite.

**2 Peter 2:17 (literary parallel).** Peter keeps the "gloom of darkness" but applies it to "wells without water, and clouds driven by a storm" (LSV), and drops the waves and stars.

**[1 Enoch 2–5; 18; 21; 80](#hl-c07-1en-2) (source tradition).** See the deep dive.

## G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

**1. Do the images reflect 1 Enoch?** Many scholars think so, given the correspondence of the four regions of nature and Jude's explicit use of 1 Enoch in the next verses. Others regard the images as drawn more generally from common Jewish and biblical imagery. The parallels with [1 Enoch 2–5](#hl-c07-1en-2) and 80 are strong enough to make the connection probable, though not certain.

**2. What are the "wandering stars"?** Planets, meteors, or stars identified with fallen angels. The Enochic background favors the last, without excluding the ordinary meaning "planets."

**3. Does "forever" imply eternal punishment?** The phrase "has been kept … throughout the age" (εἰς αἰῶνα) uses standard biblical language for permanence. As with "continuous fire" in v. 7, questions about the nature and duration of final judgment belong to the wider biblical and theological discussion. Jude's own concern is to stress the seriousness and finality of the intruders' destiny, in contrast with the readers, who await "continuous life" (v. 21).

## H. The Passage Within Jude

Verse 13 completes the application begun in v. 12. The five images (reefs, clouds, trees, waves, stars) have moved from the community's table outward through creation, and they end in darkness. The repetition of "gloom" (ζόφος) from v. 6 and of "kept" (τηρέω) from vv. 1 and 6 ties this conclusion to the beginning of Jude's argument. The intruders' fate is the fate of the rebel angels.

The verse also sets up the next section. The nature imagery of [1 Enoch 2–5](#hl-c07-1en-2) leads naturally to the prophecy of [1 Enoch 1:9](#hl-c07-1en-1), quoted in vv. 14–15, which announces the coming of the Lord to judge "all the impious." Jude moves from images to prophecy, from picture to proclamation.

## I. Contemporary Understanding

*Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.*

**Restlessness and peace.** Isaiah's sea "is not able to rest," and "There is no peace … for the wicked." Jude's wild waves may prompt reflection on how a life without God's order can be restless, churning, and productive mainly of debris. In contrast, Jude wishes his readers peace (v. 2).

**Order as gift.** The ancient view of the heavens saw order as beautiful and good. Modern readers who value freedom from constraint may find it fruitful to consider how faithfulness to God's order can be compared to a star keeping its course: not a cage, but the condition of shining.

**Guides who lead astray.** Wandering stars were useless, and dangerous, to navigators. Believers might consider whom they look to for guidance, and how to tell a reliable guide from one who has left the path. They might also consider whether their own lives are guides others can safely follow.

**The beauty of creation's obedience.** 1 Enoch, and probably Jude, invited readers to observe nature's faithfulness: rain in its season, fruit in its time, the sea within its bounds, the stars on their courses. In an age of ecological disruption, that invitation may take on new resonance. Though ancient writers did not imagine modern environmental science, the conviction that human sin and creation's disorder are connected runs through Scripture ([Gen 3:17–18](#hl-c07-gen-3); [Rom 8:19–22](#hl-c07-rom-8)). The application must be made carefully, but it is not foreign to the biblical vision.

## J. Reflection and Discussion

1. Why do you think Jude used images from nature (clouds, trees, sea, stars) to describe people? What do these images communicate that plain description could not?
2. Read [1 Enoch 2:1–5:4](#hl-c07-1en-2) and 80:2–8 (or the excerpts in this chapter). Do you find the connection with Jude 12–13 convincing? What difference does it make to your reading?
3. Isaiah says the wicked are like a sea that "is not able to rest." What forms of restlessness do you observe in contemporary life, and what might Jude's image suggest about their source?
4. Daniel pictures the faithful as stars that shine forever, and Jude pictures the intruders as stars headed for darkness. What do you think it means for a believer to "keep course" like a star?
5. How might the ancient conviction that creation displays God's order shape the way Christians relate to the natural world today?

### 1 Enoch 5 {#hl-c07-1en-5}

*R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), public domain*

**1** Observe ye how the trees cover themselves with green leaves and bear fruit: wherefore give ye heed and know with regard to all His works, and recognize how He that liveth for ever hath made them so. **2** And all His works go on thus from year to year for ever, and all the tasks which they accomplish for Him, and their tasks change not, but according as God hath ordained so is it done. **3** And behold how the sea and the rivers in like manner accomplish and change not their tasks from His commandments. **4** But ye—ye have not been steadfast, nor done the commandments of the Lord, But ye have turned away and spoken proud and hard words With your impure mouths against His greatness. Oh, ye hard-hearted, ye shall find no peace. **5** Therefore shall ye execrate your days, And the years of your life shall perish, And the years of your destruction shall be multiplied in eternal execration, And ye shall find no mercy. **6** In those days ye shall make your names an eternal execration unto all the righteous, b. And by you shall all who curse, curse, And all the sinners and godless shall imprecate by you, And all the . . . shall rejoice, e. And there shall be forgiveness of sins, f. And every mercy and peace and forbearance: g. There shall be salvation unto them, a goodly light. i. And for all of you sinners there shall be no salvation, j. But on you all shall abide a curse. **7** And for you the godless there shall be a curse. But for the elect there shall be light and joy and peace, b. And they shall inherit the earth. **8** And then there shall be bestowed upon the elect wisdom, And they shall all live and never again sin, Either through ungodliness or through pride: But they who are wise shall be humble. **9** And they shall not again transgress, Nor shall they sin all the days of their life, Nor shall they die of (the divine) anger or wrath, But they shall complete the number of the days of their life. And their lives shall be increased in peace, And the years of their joy shall be multiplied, In eternal gladness and peace, All the days of their life.

### 1 Enoch 18 {#hl-c07-1en-18}

*R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), public domain*

**1** I saw the treasuries of all the winds: I saw how He had furnished with them the whole creation and the firm foundations of the earth. **2** And I saw the corner-stone of the earth: I saw the four winds which bear [the earth and] the firmament of the heaven. **3** And I saw how the winds stretch out the vaults of heaven, and have their station between heaven and earth: these are the pillars of the heaven. **4** I saw the winds of heaven which turn and bring the circumference of the sun and all the stars to their setting. **5** I saw the winds on the earth carrying the clouds: I saw the paths of the angels. I saw at the end of the earth the firmament of the heaven above. **6** And I proceeded and saw a place which burns day and night, where there are seven mountains of magnificent stones, three towards the east, and three towards the south. **7** And as for those towards the east, one was of coloured stone, and one of pearl, and one of jacinth, and those towards the south of red stone. **8** But the middle one reached to heaven like the throne of God, of alabaster, and the summit of the throne was of sapphire. **9** And I saw a flaming fire. **10** And beyond these mountains Is a region the end of the great earth: there the heavens were completed. **11** And I saw a deep abyss, with columns of heavenly fire, and among them I saw columns of fire fall, which were beyond measure alike towards the height and towards the depth. **12** And beyond that abyss I saw a place which had no firmament of the heaven above, and no firmly founded earth beneath it: there was no water upon it, and no birds, but it was a waste and horrible place. **13** I saw there seven stars like great burning mountains, and to me, when I inquired regarding them, **14** The angel said: ‘This place is the end of heaven and earth: this has become a prison for the stars and the host of heaven. **15** And the stars which roll over the fire are they which have transgressed the commandment of the Lord in the beginning of their rising, because they did not come forth at their appointed times. **16** And He was wroth with them, and bound them till the time when their guilt should be consummated (even) for ten thousand years.’

### 1 Enoch 21 {#hl-c07-1en-21}

*R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), public domain*

**1** And I proceeded to where things were chaotic. **2** And I saw there something horrible: I saw neither a heaven above nor a firmly founded earth, but a place chaotic and horrible. **3** And there I saw seven stars of the heaven bound together in it, like great mountains and burning with fire. **4** Then I said: ‘For what sin are they bound, and on what account have they been cast in hither?’ **5** Then said Uriel, one of the holy angels, who was with me, and was chief over them, and said: ‘Enoch, why dost thou ask, and why art thou eager for the truth? **6** These are of the number of the stars of heaven, which have transgressed the commandment of the Lord, and are bound here till ten thousand years, the time entailed by their sins, are consummated.’ **7** And from thence I went to another place, which was still more horrible than the former, and I saw a horrible thing: a great fire there which burnt and blazed, and the place was cleft as far as the abyss, being full of great descending columns of fire: neither its extent or magnitude could I see, nor could I conjecture. **8** Then I said: ‘How fearful is the place and how terrible to look upon!’ **9** Then Uriel answered me, one of the holy angels who was with me, and said unto me: ‘Enoch, why hast thou such fear and affright?’ And I answered: ‘Because of this fearful place, and because of the spectacle of the pain.’ **10** And he said unto me: ‘This place is the prison of the angels, and here they will be imprisoned for ever.’

### 1 Enoch 80 {#hl-c07-1en-80}

*R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), public domain*

**1** And in those days the angel Uriel answered and said to me: ‘Behold, I have shown thee everything, Enoch, and I have revealed everything to thee that thou shouldst see this sun and this moon, and the leaders of the stars of the heaven and all those who turn them, their tasks and times and departures. **2** And in the days of the sinners the years shall be shortened, And their seed shall be tardy on their lands and fields, And all things on the earth shall alter, And shall not appear in their time: And the rain shall be kept back And the heaven shall withhold (it). **3** And in those times the fruits of the earth shall be backward, And shall not grow in their time, And the fruits of the trees shall be withheld in their time. **4** And the moon shall alter her order, And not appear at her time. **5** [And in those days the sun shall be seen and he shall journey in the evening on the extremity of the great chariot in the west] And shall shine more brightly than accords with the order of light. **6** And many chiefs of the stars shall transgress the order (prescribed). And these shall alter their orbits and tasks, And not appear at the seasons prescribed to them. **7** And the whole order of the stars shall be concealed from the sinners, And the thoughts of those on the earth shall err concerning them, [And they shall be altered from all their ways], Yea, they shall err and take them to be gods. **8** And evil shall be multiplied upon them, And punishment shall come upon them So as to destroy all.’

## B. Plain-English Orientation

Jude now quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch, the ancient patriarch who "habitually walks with God, and he is not, for God has taken him" ([Gen 5:24](#hl-c08-gen-5), LSV). The prophecy announces that the Lord comes with countless holy angels to judge everyone and to convict the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds and of all the harsh words they have spoken against him. Jude says that Enoch prophesied "to," or about, "these," the intruders. He sees the ancient prophecy as describing people in his own community.

The quotation comes from the opening chapter of the book known today as **1 Enoch**, a Jewish writing composed in stages over the last centuries before Christ. This is the only explicit quotation in Jude, and the clearest case in the New Testament of a Jewish writing from outside the Hebrew Bible being quoted and introduced as prophecy. It has raised questions from the second century to the present: Did Jude regard 1 Enoch as Scripture? What does his quotation imply about the book's authority? This chapter looks first at what the quotation says and how Jude uses it, and then turns to the questions of canon.

## C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

### ἕβδομος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ Ἑνώχ (*hebdomos apo Adam Henōch*) — ‘Enoch, the seventh from Adam’

[Genesis 5](#hl-c08-gen-5) lists the generations from Adam to Noah: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch (cf. [1 Chr 1:1–3](#hl-c08-1ch-1)). Counting Adam as the first, as ancient counting usually did, Enoch is the seventh: ἕβδομος ἀπὸ Ἀδάμ (*hebdomos apo Adam*), "seventh from Adam." The phrase appears in 1 Enoch itself, where Noah refers to his great-grandfather as "taken up, the seventh from Adam, the first man whom the Lord of Spirits created" ([1 Enoch 60:8](#hl-c08-1en-60)), and where Enoch says, "I was born the seventh in the first week" ([1 Enoch 93:3](#hl-c08-1en-93)).[^c8-1]

The description does three things:

1. **It identifies him.** There was another Enoch, Cain's son, after whom Cain named a city ([Gen 4:17](#hl-c08-gen-4)). Jude means the righteous Enoch of Seth's line.
2. **It stresses antiquity.** Enoch lived before the flood, in the seventh generation of humanity. His prophecy is among the oldest words of God imaginable. Calvin saw this as Jude's purpose: "he says expressly that he was the seventh from Adam, in order to commend the antiquity of the prophecy, because it existed in the world before the flood."[^c8-2]
3. **It may suggest completeness.** Seven was a number of fullness and perfection in Jewish thought. The "seventh" from Adam was a person of special standing, the one who "walks with God" and was taken by God. Jude does not draw attention to the symbolism, but his readers may have felt it.

Genesis says that Enoch "habitually walks with God" and that "God has taken him" ([Gen 5:24](#hl-c08-gen-5), LSV). Hebrews adds: "By faith Enoch was translated—not to see death … for before his translation he had been testified to—that he had pleased God well" ([Heb 11:5](#hl-c08-heb-11), LSV). A man so close to God and taken from the earth without dying was an ideal recipient of revelation, and Jewish tradition attributed to him visions of heaven, of the secrets of the cosmos, and of the final judgment.

### Προεφήτευσεν δὲ καὶ τούτοις (*Proephēteusen de kai toutois*) — ‘prophesied also about these’

The verb προεφήτευσεν (*proephēteusen*), "prophesied," is significant. Jude does not say that Enoch "wrote" or that "it is written." He says that Enoch prophesied. The word "also" (καί, *kai*) links this prophecy to the other evidence Jude has presented: Israel's history, the angels, Sodom, Michael, Cain, Balaam, and Korah all testify against the intruders, and so does Enoch.

The dative τούτοις (*toutois*), "to these," is best understood as "about these" or "with reference to these." Jude does not claim that Enoch foresaw these particular individuals by name. He claims that the people Enoch described, the "impious" whom the Lord will judge, are people like these. This is the same way of reading prophecy found in the Dead Sea Scrolls and elsewhere in the New Testament: ancient words are understood as speaking to the reader's own time.

### λέγων· Ἰδοὺ ἦλθεν κύριος (*legōn: Idou ēlthen kyrios*) — ‘saying: see, the Lord has come’

The quotation opens with Ἰδού (*Idou*), "Behold!" or "Look!", a prophetic call to attention.

"The LORD" translates κύριος (*kyrios*). The LSV prints it in capitals because the reference is to the God of Israel. In 1 Enoch, the subject is God: "And behold! He cometh with ten thousands of His holy ones" ([1 Enoch 1:9](#hl-c08-1en-1), trans. Charles). In Jude, however, "Lord" most often refers to Jesus (vv. 4, 17, 21; also, on some readings, v. 5). Many interpreters think Jude understands the coming Lord of Enoch's prophecy to be Jesus Christ at his return. That would be a further instance of the pattern seen in v. 5 and v. 4: language about the God of Israel applied to Jesus. The New Testament repeatedly pictures Jesus coming "with all His holy ones" ([1 Thess 3:13](#hl-c08-1th-3), LSV) and "with messengers of His power" ([2 Thess 1:7](#hl-c08-2th-1), LSV).

The verb ἦλθεν (*ēlthen*) is in the aorist, "came" (LSV: "has come"). In the context of a prophecy of future judgment, the past tense expresses certainty. Hebrew prophets often spoke of future events in the perfect tense, as though already accomplished, and Jude's Greek reproduces the effect. Some interpreters suggest that the past tense reflects the Aramaic or Greek form of Enoch that Jude knew.

### ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ (*en hagiais myriasin autou*) — ‘with his holy myriads’

The phrase ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ (*en hagiais myriasin autou*), "with his holy myriads," means "with tens of thousands of his holy ones." A μυριάς (*myrias*) is ten thousand, and the plural means "countless thousands." The "holy ones" are angels, the heavenly army that accompanies God in his appearing.

The image goes back to the theophany at Sinai, as described in Moses' blessing: "YHWH has come from Sinai, / And has risen from Seir for them; He has shone from Mount Paran, / And has come [with] myriads of holy ones" ([Deut 33:2](#hl-c08-deu-33), LSV). 1 Enoch's opening deliberately echoes this. It describes God coming to "tread upon the earth, (even) on Mount Sinai" ([1 Enoch 1:4](#hl-c08-1en-1)).[^c8-3] Zechariah also foresees the day when "my God YHWH has come in, / All holy ones [are] with You" ([Zech 14:5](#hl-c08-zec-14), LSV). Jesus speaks of the Son of Man coming "in His glory, and all the holy messengers with Him" ([Matt 25:31](#hl-c08-mat-25), LSV).

### ποιῆσαι κρίσιν κατὰ πάντων (*poiēsai krisin kata pantōn*) — ‘to execute judgment on all’

The purpose of the coming is ποιῆσαι κρίσιν κατὰ πάντων (*poiēsai krisin kata pantōn*), "to execute judgment against all." The word "all" (πᾶς, *pas*) is repeated four times in the quotation: judgment on all, convicting all, concerning all their works, concerning all the harsh words. The judgment is universal and complete. Nothing escapes.

### καὶ ἐλέγξαι πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς (*kai elenxai pantas tous asebeis*) — ‘and to convict all the impious’

The verb ἐλέγξαι (*elenxai*) means "to expose, convict, prove guilty." It is the language of a courtroom in which guilt is demonstrated. Jesus says that the Spirit "will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment" ([John 16:8](#hl-c08-jhn-16), LSV).

**A textual note.** The object of "convict" varies in the manuscripts:

| Edition | Reading | Translation |
|---|---|---|
| SBLGNT, WH, Tregelles | πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς | "all the impious" |
| Robinson–Pierpont (Byzantine), TR | πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς αὐτῶν | "all their impious ones" (LSV) |
| NA28 | πᾶσαν ψυχήν | "every soul" |

The NA28 reading, "every soul," corresponds more closely to the wording of [1 Enoch 1:9](#hl-c08-1en-1), "to convict all flesh" in Charles's translation, and the NA28 editors judged it original. The SBLGNT editors preferred "all the impious," which fits Jude's emphasis on the word "impious." The LSV follows the Byzantine reading with "their." The difference does not affect the sense of the passage: on any reading, the ungodly are convicted.[^c8-4] (The TR also reads ἐξελέγξαι, a strengthened form of the verb.)

### περὶ πάντων τῶν ἔργων ἀσεβείας αὐτῶν ὧν ἠσέβησαν (*peri pantōn tōn ergōn asebeias autōn hōn ēsebēsan*) — ‘for all the impious deeds they committed impiously’

Here the quotation reaches its most emphatic point. The Greek περὶ πάντων τῶν ἔργων ἀσεβείας αὐτῶν ὧν ἠσέβησαν (*peri pantōn tōn ergōn asebeias autōn hōn ēsebēsan*) uses the root ἀσεβ- (*aseb-*), "ungodly," twice in quick succession: "their ungodly works which they ungodly did." With "impious" earlier and "impious sinners" at the end, the word family appears four times in a single sentence. The verb ἠσέβησαν (*ēsebēsan*), "they acted impiously," occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.

The repetition is deliberate. Jude introduced the intruders as ἀσεβεῖς, "impious," in v. 4. Now, in the words of the ancient prophecy, the same word rings out four times. Jude's earlier description of them was not merely his own opinion. It was the language of prophecy.

### καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ’ αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς (*kai peri pantōn tōn sklērōn hōn elalēsan kat’ autou hamartōloi asebeis*) — ‘and for all the harsh things impious sinners have spoken against him’

The last clause shifts from deeds to words: περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ' αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς (*peri pantōn tōn sklērōn hōn elalēsan kat' autou hamartōloi asebeis*), "concerning all the hard things that ungodly sinners spoke against him." The adjective σκληρός (*sklēros*) means "hard, harsh, rough." In context it means defiant, insolent speech against God.

1 Enoch returns to this theme repeatedly. Immediately after the prophecy, it accuses sinners: "ye have turned away and spoken proud and hard words / With your impure mouths against His greatness" ([1 Enoch 5:4](#hl-c08-1en-5)). It speaks of a valley of judgment for those "who utter with their lips against the Lord unseemly words and of His glory speak hard things" (27:2), and it charges, "ye spake proud and insolent words against His righteousness" (101:3).[^c8-5]

The emphasis on speech connects the quotation with Jude's charges. The intruders "speak evil of glorious [ones]" (v. 8) and of "whatever [things] they have not known" (v. 10). In the next verse Jude will add that "their mouth speaks swollen words" (v. 16), and the apostles foretold "scoffers" (v. 18). Sins of speech run through the letter.

### Comparing Jude 14–15 with 1 Enoch 1:9

Placing Jude's quotation beside R. H. Charles's translation of [1 Enoch 1:9](#hl-c08-1en-1) (which Charles made from the Ethiopic, compared with the Greek) shows both close agreement and some differences:

| Jude 14–15 (LSV) | 1 Enoch 1:9 (trans. Charles) |
|---|---|
| "Behold, the LORD has come" | "And behold! He cometh" |
| "with myriads of His holy ones," | "with ten thousands of ⌈His⌉ holy ones" |
| "to do judgment against all," | "To execute judgement upon all," |
| — | "And to destroy ⌈all⌉ the ungodly:" |
| "and to convict all their impious ones," | "And to convict all flesh" |
| "concerning all their works of impiety that they did impiously," | "Of all the works ⌈of their ungodliness⌉ which they have ungodly committed," |
| "and concerning all the harsh [words] that impious sinners spoke against Him." | "⌈And of all the hard things which⌉ ungodly sinners ⌈have spoken⌉ against Him." |

The differences are of three kinds:

1. **Jude names "the Lord"** where 1 Enoch has "He." This may be Jude's clarification, and it opens the way to applying the prophecy to Christ.
2. **Jude lacks the line "And to destroy all the ungodly,"** found in the Ethiopic and Greek of [1 Enoch.
3](#hl-c08-1en-3). **"All flesh" vs. "the impious."** The NA28 reading, "every soul," is close to 1 Enoch's "all flesh," which is one reason the NA28 editors adopted it.

The Aramaic original of 1 Enoch survives only in fragments from Qumran Cave 4. The complete book survives only in Ge'ez, and a Greek translation of chapters 1–32 survives in a manuscript found at Akhmim in Egypt.[^c8-6] How exactly Jude's wording relates to these versions is debated, and this book does not try to settle it. Earlier commentators already weighed the evidence. Alfred Plummer noted that the Book of Enoch has a counterpart to "the hard things which sinners have spoken against God," and judged this "almost conclusive" against the theory that a later writer copied the prophecy from Jude into Enoch: "If so, why did he not copy it exactly?" The Cambridge commentary judged it "more natural to suppose that he quoted here, as in previous instances, what he thought edifying" than to adopt theories of an independent tradition or a special inspiration.[^c8-7] What is clear is that Jude quotes a form of the text very close to the one we know, adapting it to his purpose.

### Deep dive: The Book of Enoch and the biblical canon

Jude's quotation of Enoch raises one of the most interesting questions in the history of the Bible: what does it mean when a biblical writer quotes a book that is not itself in most Bibles?

#### 1. What is 1 Enoch?

"1 Enoch" (also called "Ethiopic Enoch") is a collection of five main sections, written by Jewish authors at different times between roughly the third century BC and the turn of the era:

| Section | Chapters | Content | Approximate date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Book of the Watchers | 1–36 | Coming judgment; fall of the Watchers; Enoch's journeys | 3rd century BC or earlier |
| Book of Parables (Similitudes) | 37–71 | Visions of the "Son of Man" / "Elect One" and judgment | 1st century BC–1st century AD (debated) |
| Astronomical Book | 72–82 | Movements of sun, moon, and stars; calendar | 3rd century BC or earlier |
| Book of Dreams | 83–90 | Visions of the flood and of Israel's history (the "Animal Apocalypse") | 2nd century BC |
| Epistle of Enoch | 91–108 | Exhortations, woes, the "Apocalypse of Weeks" | 2nd century BC |

The quotation in Jude comes from the opening of the Book of the Watchers, one of the oldest parts.[^c8-8]

**How the text survives.** Aramaic fragments of most parts of 1 Enoch were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls in Qumran Cave 4 (manuscripts known as 4Q201–4Q212). The oldest are dated by their handwriting to the early second century BC. The Book of Parables is not represented at Qumran, which is one reason it is often dated later. A Greek manuscript of chapters 1–32, found at Akhmim (ancient Panopolis) in Egypt and published in 1892, preserves the Greek translation, and other Greek fragments survive. The complete book survives only in **Ge'ez**, the classical language of Ethiopia, in which it has been transmitted as part of the Bible.[^c8-9]

**Canonical status today.** 1 Enoch is part of the Old Testament in the **Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church** and the **Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church**. It is used by the Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jewish) community. It is not part of the canon of Rabbinic Judaism or of other Christian churches, whether Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox outside Ethiopia and Eritrea, or Protestant.[^c8-10]

#### 2. How did early Christians respond to Jude's quotation?

The ancient church took up the question directly, and its answers diverged:

- **Tertullian** (c. 200) argued that the Book of Enoch should be accepted. He acknowledged that "the Scripture of Enoch … is not received by some, because it is not admitted into the Jewish canon either," but he insisted that "Enoch possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude."[^c8-11] For Tertullian, Jude's quotation proved Enoch's authority.
- **Jerome** (late fourth century) reported the opposite effect: "because in it he quotes from the apocryphal Book of Enoch it is rejected by many. Nevertheless by age and use it has gained authority and is reckoned among the Holy Scriptures."[^c8-12] For some, Jude's quotation of Enoch counted against Jude.
- **Augustine** (early fifth century) took a middle position: "We cannot deny that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, left some divine writings, for this is asserted by the Apostle Jude in his canonical epistle. But it is not without reason that these writings have no place in that canon of Scripture which was preserved in the temple of the Hebrew people." He explained that such books are excluded because of their "obscure origin" and because "though there is some truth in these apocryphal writings, yet they contain so many false statements."[^c8-13]
- **John Calvin** (sixteenth century) suggested that Jude might not have taken the prophecy from a book at all: "I rather think that this prophecy was unwritten, than that it was taken from an apocryphal book; for it may have been delivered down by memory to posterity by the ancients."[^c8-14]

#### 3. How can Jude's use be understood?

Modern interpreters generally take one of the following views. They are presented here with their strengths and weaknesses.

**(a) Jude regarded 1 Enoch as Scripture.** On this view, Jude, like some Jews of his time (the Qumran community preserved many copies of Enoch), treated 1 Enoch as authoritative revelation.

- *Strength:* Jude calls the passage prophecy and uses it as decisive evidence.
- *Weakness:* Jude does not use the formulas by which New Testament writers usually introduce Scripture ("it is written," "the Scripture says"). And the book was not, as far as we know, part of the scriptures generally recognized in the synagogues.

**(b) Jude regarded this prophecy as a genuine word of Enoch, without endorsing the whole book.** On this view, Jude believed that the historical Enoch spoke these words, which had been preserved in tradition and recorded in the Enochic literature, without implying that everything in 1 Enoch was inspired.

- *Strength:* This view takes Jude's "Enoch … prophesied" seriously and matches Augustine's position.
- *Weakness:* Modern historical study regards 1 Enoch as written many centuries after any historical Enoch. Those who hold this view must either dispute that conclusion or argue that the book preserves an ancient tradition. Both are possible but hard to demonstrate.

**(c) Jude quoted a respected text that his readers knew, as true in what it says, without making a claim about its authorship or canonical status.** On this view, "prophesied" means that the passage speaks truly about the future judgment, as indeed the Old Testament does in many places ([Deut 33:2](#hl-c08-deu-33); [Zech 14:5](#hl-c08-zec-14); [Dan 7:10](#hl-c08-dan-7)). Jude quotes it because it was familiar and authoritative *to his readers*, and possibly to the intruders themselves, if they appealed to visionary literature.

- *Strength:* The New Testament elsewhere quotes non-biblical sources for true statements without implying their inspiration. Paul quotes a Greek poet at Athens: "as certain of your poets have also said: For we are also His offspring" ([Acts 17:28](#hl-c08-act-17), LSV). Writing to Titus, he even calls the Cretan poet Epimenides "a prophet of their own" before quoting him and adding, "This testimony is true" ([Titus 1:12–13](#hl-c08-tit-1), LSV). He quotes a proverb found in the Greek playwright Menander: "evil communications corrupt good manners" ([1 Cor 15:33](#hl-c08-1co-15), LSV). Second Timothy names Moses' opponents "Jannes and Jambres" ([2 Tim 3:8](#hl-c08-2ti-3), LSV), names known from Jewish tradition and not from the Old Testament.
- *Weakness:* Jude's language is stronger than these parallels. He says Enoch "prophesied," and he treats the prophecy as applying directly to the intruders.

#### 4. Principles worth holding

Whatever view one takes, several principles help readers think clearly:

1. **Quotation is not canonization.** That a biblical author quotes a book does not make that book Scripture. Paul's quotations of pagan poets do not make those poets canonical. The question of Jude's view of Enoch must be decided on its own evidence.
2. **The quoted statement can be true without endorsing everything in the source.** Jude affirms that the Lord will come with his holy ones in judgment, a truth taught throughout Scripture. Nothing in his quotation requires readers to accept the astronomical calendar of [1 Enoch 72–82](#hl-c08-1en-72-82) or every detail of its angelology.
3. **Jude's own authority does not depend on the answer.** The church accepted Jude into its canon in full knowledge that Jude quoted Enoch, as Tertullian, Jerome, and Augustine show. Christians who accept Jude as Scripture can hold different views of [1 Enoch.
4](#hl-c08-1en-4). **The study of 1 Enoch illuminates the New Testament.** Whatever its canonical status, 1 Enoch helps modern readers understand ideas that were current in Jude's world: the Watchers, the judgment of fallen angels, the "Son of Man," and the coming of God with holy myriads. Reading it is no threat to faith. It is a way of hearing the New Testament in its own historical accent.
5. **Respect for other traditions.** For Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Christians, 1 Enoch is Scripture. Other Christians can respect that tradition while explaining their own canon, and can recognize that the boundaries of the canon were not settled in the same way or at the same time everywhere.

## D. Original-Language Investigation

| Greek | Transliteration | Basic meaning | In context | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ἕβδομος | *hebdomos* | seventh | "the seventh from Adam" | Inclusive counting; 1 Enoch 60:8; 93:3. |
| προφητεύω | *prophēteuō* | prophesy | "prophesied" | Not "wrote" or "it is written." |
| τούτοις | *toutois* | to/about these | "to these" | Dative of reference. |
| ἰδού | *idou* | behold, look | "Behold" | Prophetic call to attention. |
| ἦλθεν | *ēlthen* | came | "has come" | Aorist expressing certainty. |
| μυριάς | *myrias* | ten thousand | "myriads" | Countless angelic host. |
| ἅγιος | *hagios* | holy | "holy ones" | Angels (Deut 33:2; Zech 14:5). |
| κρίσις | *krisis* | judgment | "judgment" | |
| ἐλέγχω | *elenchō* | expose, convict | "to convict" | TR: ἐξελέγχω. |
| ἀσεβής / ἀσέβεια / ἀσεβέω | *asebēs* / *asebeia* / *asebeō* | impious / impiety / act impiously | "impious … impiety … did impiously" | Fourfold repetition; ἀσεβέω is an NT hapax. |
| σκληρός | *sklēros* | hard, harsh | "harsh [words]" | Insolent speech; cf. 1 Enoch 5:4; 27:2. |
| ἁμαρτωλός | *hamartōlos* | sinner | "sinners" | |
| πᾶσαν ψυχήν | *pasan psychēn* | every soul | (NA28 reading) | Alternative to "all the impious." |

**On "prophesied."** The verb προφητεύω has a range of uses in the New Testament: foretelling ([Matt 15:7](#hl-c08-mat-15)), speaking God's message ([1 Cor 14:1–5](#hl-c08-1co-14)), and even mocking demands to "prophesy" ([Mark 14:65](#hl-c08-mrk-14)). In Jude, it clearly means that Enoch's words convey a true message about the future judgment of the ungodly. Whether it also implies a judgment about the book's authorship and authority is the question discussed in the deep dive.

## E. The Historical and Cultural World

**Enoch traditions in Judaism.** Enoch fascinated Jewish writers of the Second Temple period. Apart from 1 Enoch, he appears in *Jubilees*, in the Dead Sea Scrolls, and in later works such as *2 Enoch* (preserved in Slavonic) and *3 Enoch* (Hebrew). He was celebrated as a scribe, a sage, a recipient of heavenly secrets, and a witness to the coming judgment. Jude's readers, who knew the Watcher story (v. 6) and probably the nature images of 1 Enoch (vv. 12–13), evidently regarded Enoch as a significant voice.

**Fluid boundaries.** In Jude's day, the boundaries of the Jewish scriptures were not settled in every detail, especially at the margins of the "Writings." The Qumran community preserved many copies of 1 Enoch and Jubilees alongside biblical books. Other Jewish groups, and later the rabbinic tradition, did not treat these books as Scripture. Early Christians inherited this situation, and their own canonical lists took several centuries to stabilize. Jude's quotation should be read against that background, not anachronistically against later definitions.

**Prophecy as present-tense interpretation.** Jewish interpreters of the period frequently read ancient prophecies as referring to their own time. The Dead Sea Scrolls' commentaries (the *pesharim*) quote a prophetic text and then explain its "interpretation" in terms of the community's experience. Jude's "Enoch … prophesied to these" is the same kind of reading.

## F. Connections Across Scripture

**[Genesis 5:21–24](#hl-c08-gen-5); [Hebrews 11:5](#hl-c08-heb-11) (Enoch).** The biblical basis for Enoch's reputation. Hebrews celebrates his faith and translation.

**[Deuteronomy 33:2](#hl-c08-deu-33) (source of the imagery).** The coming of the LORD "[with] myriads of holy ones" at Sinai is the ultimate source of the picture in [1 Enoch 1:9](#hl-c08-1en-1) and Jude 14.

**[Zechariah 14:5](#hl-c08-zec-14); [Daniel 7:10](#hl-c08-dan-7) (shared theme).** The coming of God with his holy ones to judge.

**[Matthew 25:31](#hl-c08-mat-25); [Mark 8:38](#hl-c08-mrk-8); 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 2 Thessalonians 1:7 (shared theme).** The return of Jesus with his angels. If Jude understands "the Lord" in the quotation to be Jesus, these texts are his closest New Testament parallels.

**[Acts 17:28](#hl-c08-act-17); [Titus 1:12–13](#hl-c08-tit-1); 1 Corinthians 15:33; 2 Timothy 3:8 (method).** New Testament quotations of, and allusions to, non-biblical sources. These help frame the question of what Jude's quotation implies.

**[John 16:8](#hl-c08-jhn-16) (vocabulary).** The Spirit "will convict" (ἐλέγξει, *elenxei*) the world, the same verb as Jude's "to convict."

## G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

**1. Did Jude regard 1 Enoch as Scripture?** Discussed in the deep dive. Interpreters remain divided. The most cautious conclusion is that Jude regarded this prophecy as a true word of God about judgment, and that his readers recognized it as authoritative. The question of what Jude thought about the book as a whole cannot be answered from his single quotation.

**2. Who is "the Lord" in v. 14?** God in 1 Enoch. Most likely Jesus in Jude's application, given Jude's usage elsewhere and the New Testament's expectation of Christ's coming with his angels.

**3. Which text did Jude use?** Probably a Greek or Aramaic form of 1 Enoch close to the ones we know, perhaps with his own adaptations. The exact relationship is debated.

**4. Which reading is original in v. 15?** "All the impious" (SBLGNT), "all their impious ones" (Byzantine), or "every soul" (NA28). The meaning is the same in substance.

**5. Does Jude's use of Enoch undermine his authority?** Some early Christians thought so. The church as a whole concluded otherwise. Modern readers who share the church's acceptance of Jude can read his quotation as an example of how the Spirit used the literature and traditions of the time to speak a true word, without thereby endorsing everything in that literature.

## H. The Passage Within Jude

The Enoch quotation is the centerpiece of Jude's case. It supplies the clearest example of the judgment "written beforehand" (v. 4), and its fourfold "impious" confirms that Jude's description of the intruders was the language of prophecy. It is followed by another application ("These are…," v. 16), which applies the prophecy's charge of "harsh words" to the intruders' grumbling and arrogant speech.

The quotation also provides the letter's main picture of the future: the Lord coming with his holy ones. The readers, by contrast, are told to wait for "the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 21) and are promised that God will set them "in the presence of His glory unblemished" (v. 24). The same coming that brings judgment on the impious brings mercy and joy to those who have been kept.

## I. Contemporary Understanding

*Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.*

**Reading Scripture with its world.** Jude's quotation of Enoch shows that the New Testament was written in conversation with the literature and traditions of its time. Modern readers may find their understanding enriched, not threatened, by learning about that world: the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Jewish writings of the Second Temple period, and the history of the canon.

**Humility about the canon.** Christians today hold different views about which books belong in the Old Testament (Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox, and Ethiopian canons differ). Jude's quotation of Enoch, and the varied responses of Tertullian, Jerome, Augustine, and Calvin, may encourage both conviction about one's own tradition and charity toward others.

**Words matter to God.** Enoch's prophecy convicts sinners not only of their deeds but of "the harsh [words]" they have spoken against God. Jude's letter is full of concern about speech: slander, harsh words, grumbling, boasting, scoffing. In an age of easy and often harsh public speech, the passage may prompt reflection on accountability for words.

**The coming of the Lord.** The picture of the Lord coming with countless holy ones is both a warning and a comfort. It warns that injustice and ungodliness will not have the last word. It comforts those who wait for "the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 21).

## J. Reflection and Discussion

1. How did you react to learning that Jude quotes a book not found in most Bibles? Did it raise questions for you, and how would you begin to answer them?
2. Compare Jude's use of Enoch with Paul's quotations of Greek poets ([Acts 17:28](#hl-c08-act-17); [Titus 1:12](#hl-c08-tit-1); [1 Cor 15:33](#hl-c08-1co-15)). What similarities and differences do you see?
3. Tertullian, Jerome, Augustine, and Calvin each responded differently to Jude's quotation. Which response do you find most persuasive, and why?
4. Enoch's prophecy emphasizes "harsh [words] … spoken against Him." Why might speech be singled out alongside deeds in a description of ungodliness?
5. How does the picture of the Lord coming "with myriads of His holy ones" shape your hope and your sense of responsibility?

שָׁנָה וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה **24** וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֵינֶנּוּ כִּי־לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים **25** וַיְחִי מְתוּשֶׁלַח שֶׁבַע וּשְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה וּמְאַת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד אֶת־לָמֶךְ **26** וַיְחִי מְתוּשֶׁלַח אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת־לֶמֶךְ שְׁתַּיִם וּשְׁמוֹנִים שָׁנָה וּשְׁבַע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת **27** וַיִּהְיוּ כָּל־יְמֵי מְתוּשֶׁלַח תֵּשַׁע וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וּתְשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיָּמֹת **28** וַיְחִי־לֶמֶךְ שְׁתַּיִם וּשְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה וּמְאַת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד בֵּן **29** וַיִּקְרָא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ נֹחַ לֵאמֹר זֶה יְנַחֲמֵנוּ מִמַּעֲשֵׂנוּ וּמֵעִצְּבוֹן יָדֵינוּ מִן־הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר אֵרְרָהּ יְהוָה **30** וַיְחִי־לֶמֶךְ אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת־נֹחַ חָמֵשׁ וְתִשְׁעִים שָׁנָה וַחֲמֵשׁ מֵאֹת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת **31** וַיְהִי כָּל־יְמֵי־לֶמֶךְ שֶׁבַע וְשִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה וּשְׁבַע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיָּמֹת **32** וַיְהִי־נֹחַ בֶּן־חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד נֹחַ אֶת־שֵׁם אֶת־חָם וְאֶת־יָפֶת
:::

*English (BSB)*

**1** This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, He made him in His own likeness. **2** Male and female He created them, and He blessed them. And in the day they were created, He called them “man.” **3** When Adam was 130 years old, he had a son in his own likeness, after his own image; and he named him Seth. **4** And after he had become the father of Seth, Adam lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. **5** So Adam lived a total of 930 years, and then he died. **6** When Seth was 105 years old, he became the father of Enosh. **7** And after he had become the father of Enosh, Seth lived 807 years and had other sons and daughters. **8** So Seth lived a total of 912 years, and then he died. **9** When Enosh was 90 years old, he became the father of Kenan. **10** And after he had become the father of Kenan, Enosh lived 815 years and had other sons and daughters. **11** So Enosh lived a total of 905 years, and then he died. **12** When Kenan was 70 years old, he became the father of Mahalalel. **13** And after he had become the father of Mahalalel, Kenan lived 840 years and had other sons and daughters. **14** So Kenan lived a total of 910 years, and then he died. **15** When Mahalalel was 65 years old, he became the father of Jared. **16** And after he had become the father of Jared, Mahalalel lived 830 years and had other sons and daughters. **17** So Mahalalel lived a total of 895 years, and then he died. **18** When Jared was 162 years old, he became the father of Enoch. **19** And after he had become the father of Enoch, Jared lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. **20** So Jared lived a total of 962 years, and then he died. **21** When Enoch was 65 years old, he became the father of Methuselah. **22** And after he had become the father of Methuselah, Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters. **23** So Enoch lived a total of 365 years. **24** Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away. **25** When Methuselah was 187 years old, he became the father of Lamech. **26** And after he had become the father of Lamech, Methuselah lived 782 years and had other sons and daughters. **27** So Methuselah lived a total of 969 years, and then he died. **28** When Lamech was 182 years old, he had a son. **29** And he named him Noah, saying, “May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed.” **30** And after he had become the father of Noah, Lamech lived 595 years and had other sons and daughters. **31** So Lamech lived a total of 777 years, and then he died. **32** After Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

*English (WEB)*

**1** This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness. **2** He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them Adam. **3** Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. **4** The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he became the father of other sons and daughters. **5** All the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, then he died. **6** Seth lived one hundred five years, then became the father of Enosh. **7** Seth lived after he became the father of Enosh eight hundred seven years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. **8** All of the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, then he died. **9** Enosh lived ninety years, and became the father of Kenan. **10** Enosh lived after he became the father of Kenan eight hundred fifteen years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. **11** All of the days of Enosh were nine hundred five years, then he died. **12** Kenan lived seventy years, then became the father of Mahalalel. **13** Kenan lived after he became the father of Mahalalel eight hundred forty years, and became the father of other sons and daughters **14** and all of the days of Kenan were nine hundred ten years, then he died. **15** Mahalalel lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Jared. **16** Mahalalel lived after he became the father of Jared eight hundred thirty years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. **17** All of the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred ninety-five years, then he died. **18** Jared lived one hundred sixty-two years, then became the father of Enoch. **19** Jared lived after he became the father of Enoch eight hundred years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. **20** All of the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty-two years, then he died. **21** Enoch lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Methuselah. **22** After Methuselah’s birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and became the father of more sons and daughters. **23** All the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years. **24** Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him. **25** Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years, then became the father of Lamech. **26** Methuselah lived after he became the father of Lamech seven hundred eighty-two years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. **27** All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty-nine years, then he died. **28** Lamech lived one hundred eighty-two years, then became the father of a son. **29** He named him Noah, saying, “This one will comfort us in our work and in the toil of our hands, caused by the ground which the LORD has cursed.” **30** Lamech lived after he became the father of Noah five hundred ninety-five years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. **31** All the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy-seven years, then he died. **32** Noah was five hundred years old, then Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
